entry.title: SIX MONTHS OF FRUSTRATION, DISCHARGED IN ONE SWING — RILEY TURNS A NINE-AND-NINETY-MILE BULLET FROM PHILADELPHIA'S CLOSER INTO THREE EIGHTH-INNING RUNS, AND THE OLD OCTOBER ORDER IS OVERTURNED: BRAVES 5, QUAKERS 3
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 84 · Wednesday, the Thirtieth of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 4 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

SIX MONTHS OF FRUSTRATION, DISCHARGED IN ONE SWING — RILEY TURNS A NINE-AND-NINETY-MILE BULLET FROM PHILADELPHIA'S CLOSER INTO THREE EIGHTH-INNING RUNS, AND THE OLD OCTOBER ORDER IS OVERTURNED: BRAVES 5, QUAKERS 3

The opener at Truist Park is a seesaw of triples and nerve — Sale rises from his bed at dawn and strikes out nine, Luzardo makes a mockery of the word 'opener' with five sparkling innings, Realmuto's two-run three-bagger has Philadelphia ahead in the seventh — until Riley, with two out and two aboard in the eighth, meets Duran's 99.9-mile fastball and deposits it in the right-center seats, whereupon a club beaten by these same Quakers in three straight Octobers finds itself one victory from the Division Series

The first October afternoon at Truist Park was an argument that changed hands four times, and it ended on the fastest pitch Jhoan Duran could summon. Austin Riley — whose summer, by his own club's accounting, was six months of frustration in search of an afternoon like this one — came to the plate in the eighth with two out, two aboard, and Atlanta trailing 3-2. Duran reached back for 99.9 miles the hour. Riley met it flush and sent it to the right-center seats, and the yard shook, and the verdict was written: 5-3, Atlanta, and the first blood of the Wild Card round.

It was a proper duel long before it was a thunderclap. Chris Sale, making his first postseason start in five years, confessed he had been awake since first light — "I could have pitched this game at 8:15 this morning," said the ancient left-hander, and he pitched it at two o'clock like a man renewed: six and one-third innings, four hits, nine strikeouts, Harper fanned along the way with heat that touched three figures. Opposite him, Jesús Luzardo made comedy of the caution in his manager's vocabulary. Mattingly had called him an opener; the left-hander, whose whole September amounted to one four-pitch inning, gave five innings of three-hit, one-run pitching with six strikeouts, and handed the game over with Philadelphia ahead 1-0 on Bohm's first-inning double.

The middle chapters belonged to the three-baggers. Yastrzemski's single squared it in the second; Albies tripled home Harris in the sixth for 2-1; and in the seventh Realmuto answered with a two-run triple of his own — De La Cruz and Stott scampering home, 3-2 Philadelphia, and the visitors nine outs from the precise script of their last three October meetings with this club, every one of which the Quakers had won. Then came the eighth: Harris, three hits on the day, singled once more; Albies followed him aboard; and Riley closed the ledger. Lee took the win in relief, Iglesias closed the ninth, and Duran — an All-Star all summer — wore the loss and the blown save together.

The arithmetic of the best-of-three is now brutally simple. Atlanta, which took nine of thirteen from Philadelphia this season and had never beaten them in October, leads one game to none and can end the affair this very afternoon: Game Two goes at two o'clock at Truist Park, Sánchez (18-7, a 2.91 figure) — fully rested, as this paper noted in yesterday's armory — against Mahle (7-10, 3.99). The survivor of the series calls upon the hundred-win Dodgers when the Division Series opens Saturday, the third of October; the Quakers, for their part, must now win twice in two days or watch a fifth consecutive October end at its first station.

The Postseason Card

THE STUMBLE AT THE DUGOUT STEP IS THE ONLY ONE ALL EVENING — ANTONACCI TRIPS AT THE INTRODUCTIONS, THEN TREADS ON HOUSTON FOR NINE INNINGS: WHITE STOCKINGS 6, HOUSTONS 3

The 84-win guests arrive at the 81-win champions' yard and play the part of the better club from the first frame — three runs before the second inning is done, Colson Montgomery's thunderclap in the fourth, and a bullpen relay that ends with young Taylor emptying the tank across a career-long two and one-third — while in the eighth the hosts' last uprising dies at the feet of Yainer Diaz, and word arrives that the Vatican itself had written the South Side ahead of the series

The evening's augury came at the pregame introductions, when Sam Antonacci tripped running out of the dugout at Daikin Park — and it proved a false omen entirely, for that misstep was very nearly Chicago's last. The White Stockings, whose 84 victories exceed their hosts' 81 — the curiosity this paper has twice remarked now made flesh — struck the champions of the West early and never surrendered the lead: Murakami's sacrifice fly cashed Antonacci in the first, and in the second Antonacci himself lined a single that brought home Braden Montgomery and Meidroth both, 3-0, before Houston's relay of arms had found its footing. The opener Blubaugh, undone by three walks in two-thirds of an inning, wore the loss; his successor King was raked for four hits in a third.

Colson Montgomery's solo thunderbolt in the fourth made it 4-0, Meidroth singled home a fifth in the fifth, and when Velázquez answered with a two-run blast for Houston, Murakami came home on a wild pitch to restore the four-run distance. The arithmetic thereafter belonged to Chicago's bullpen — Smith opening with three spotless innings, Hicks taking the win — and above all to Grant Taylor, summoned with two out in the seventh, who in the eighth met the evening's one true crisis — runners at first and second, two out, a three-run lead, and the dangerous Diaz at the plate — and put out the fire and finished the game besides: two and one-third innings, five strikeouts, the longest outing of his young life. Houston's final tally required an error to score. And for benediction, the club revealed that Pope Leo XIV — a White Sox man of long standing, who sat in the Rate Field seats for the 2005 World Series against these very Astros — had sent a letter to the chairman Reinsdorf ahead of the series, commending the club's fostering of friendship and solidarity through sport. The South Side, it appears, holds accounts in every ledger.

So a club that had not played an October game since 2021 leads its series one game to none, and the champions of the West — who took five of seven from Chicago this summer, and whose season was saved from a 20-31 May by main strength — stand in a must-win posture at their own yard. Game Two goes at five o'clock this evening at Daikin Park: Burke (11-7, 3.34) for the visitors against Brown (6-4, 3.19), the erstwhile invalid, for the hosts. The survivor of the series travels to Cleveland, where the Division Series opens Saturday, the third of October.

TWO SONS OF MASSACHUSETTS BREAK NEW ENGLAND'S HEART IN THE BRONX — SCHLITTLER STRIKES OUT TEN, RICE STRIKES A GRAND SLAM, AND THE OLDEST QUARREL OPENS AT NINE TO NOTHING: BRONX BOMBERS 9, CRIMSON HOSE 0

The seventh October chapter of the game's oldest feud begins as a taut 2-0 affair and ends an avalanche — Schlittler, who closed Boston's season a year ago, gives six and one-third two-hit innings; Rice, faithful to his scrambled eggs and avocado toast, collects four hits, two home runs, and six runs driven in; young Lombard makes a three-hit postseason debut; and Boston's miseries multiply when Anthony departs the sixth with the old right hand barking anew

New York's Game One plan was executed by two men raised in the shadow of the enemy's cathedral. Cam Schlittler and Ben Rice, Massachusetts boys the both, grew up surrounded by everything Red Sox — and in the seventh postseason meeting of the game's oldest quarrel they dismantled the club of their boyhood with a thoroughness that will be remembered on both sides of the line. Schlittler, owner of the American's best earned-run figure at 1.95 and the man who ended Boston's season in last October's Game Three, gave six and one-third innings of two-hit, scoreless pitching with ten strikeouts; Rice, a man of iron routine — the same cage work daily, the same breakfast of scrambled eggs and avocado toast — went four for five with a double, a fifth-inning home run, and, for punctuation, an eighth-inning grand slam: six runs driven in on the night.

For six innings it was nonetheless a duel worthy of the rivalry. Payton Tolle — at three-and-twenty the third-youngest man ever to start a Boston postseason opener, as this paper recorded yesterday, behind only Wood of 1912 and Ruth of 1918 — acquitted himself with honor: four and two-thirds innings, one run, the game still within a swing's reach at 2-0 when he departed. Then the Boston bullpen came apart at the seams — two in the seventh, five in the eighth, the last four aboard Rice's slam — while Wells drove home two and George Lombard Jr., the boy wonder whose first big-league hit, this very summer, was a home run, rapped three hits in his first taste of October. "Locked in," his teammates called him; the box score concurs.

Boston's deeper wound may be the one in the sixth inning's margin: Roman Anthony, checked swings having set the old right hand to barking, left the game and was hit for by Monasterio — the same hand whose partially torn ring-finger tendon cost him a stretch of the summer. "Hard to say right now," said the manager Tracy of his availability for Game Two, and the club must weigh the crueler arithmetic of an injury replacement, which would bar him until the Championship Series. There was one entry on the credit side of Boston's ward ledger: the ace Crochet, unseen since April, was formally activated from the sixty-day rolls on the eve of the series, the crate at last unsealed. He may be needed at once — Game Two goes at eight o'clock this evening in the Bronx, the wins leader Gray (18-5, 2.72) against Fried (5-5, 2.80), with the survivor of the series bound for Tampa Bay and Saturday's Division Series, and Boston bound for winter if it cannot solve the Bombers twice running.

SEVEN INNINGS WITHOUT A HIT UNTIL A DRIBBLER SPOILS THE SCROLL — KING FLIRTS WITH OCTOBER IMMORTALITY, THREE THUNDERCLAPS DO THE REST, AND MUSGROVE WALKS OUT OF TWO LOST YEARS INTO A ROARING PETCO NIGHT: GASLAMP NINE 8, CUBS 0

Last October's tormentors are made to pay for it with interest — Tatis and Machado strike home runs before the first inning is out, Bogaerts adds a third, and King carries a no-hitter to one out in the seventh, the longest such October errand since 2019, before Hoerner's forty-foot roller writes the only line in Chicago's hit column against him; then, with the verdict long settled, the hometown right-hander Musgrove takes a big-league mound for the first time since 2024 and the Gaslamp Quarter forgets the score entirely

San Diego opened its October by settling last year's account with compound interest. The Cubs, who ejected the Friars from the Wild Card round a year ago and had taken five of six from them in the season just closed, were handed the most comprehensive defeat of the young postseason: 8-0, thirteen hits against three, and for seven innings the genuine prospect of an ignominy without precedent in their October annals. Michael King, handed a 2-0 lead before the first inning was done, carried a no-hitter into the seventh inning — the longest postseason no-hit bid since Aníbal Sánchez's seven and two-thirds in the 2019 Championship Series — until, with one out, Hoerner topped a forty-foot dribbler down the third-base line that no arm in the yard could have converted. "When you're going out in the seventh with a no-hitter — you definitely are thinking about it," King allowed afterward. His final line wanted nothing for the loss of the scroll: seven innings, the one hit, eight strikeouts, and heat that touched 97.6 — his liveliest in three years.

The thunder had come early and kept its own counsel. Tatis opened the home first with a home run and Machado followed him two batters later with another — 2-0 before the Gaslamp crowd had settled — and the pair kept at it: Machado's double cashed Tatis in the third, Bogaerts struck the third homer in the fourth, and a five-spot's worth of industry in the middle innings (Merrill's two-run single and a passed ball among the freight) ran it to seven. Boyd, Chicago's Game One starter, was charged with three home runs inside four innings and the loss. The Cubs' three hits were their fewest consolation; their ace question now presses, for the sore-shouldered Gausman — whose non-throwing shoulder this paper reported under the trainers' watch — takes the ball tonight after all.

The ninth inning belonged to sentiment. Joe Musgrove, the San Diegan who had not stood on a big-league mound since 2024 — activated from the sixty-day rolls only this week after the long road back — walked out of two lost years and into a roaring Petco night, and worked a scoreless ninth around two hits and a walk, striking out a pair, while the score ceased to matter to anyone in the yard. The series stands one game to none for the Gaslamp nine; Game Two goes at ten o'clock this evening at Petco Park, Gausman (9-12, 4.51) against Pivetta (3-2, 2.86), whose own summer was five months lost to a flexor strain. The survivor travels to Milwaukee and its hundred-three-win hosts for Saturday's Division Series; the Cubs must now take two straight from a club they could not touch for seven innings.

News Around the League

THE CAPTAIN'S CASE, DECIDED: JUDGE IS LEFT OFF THE WILD CARD ROLLS — ALL HIS CONVINCING COULD NOT OUTRUN A CALF THAT WANTS THREE WEEKS, THOUGH STANTON AND GRISHAM RETURN TO THE COLORS

The verdict this paper promised its readers arrived before the Bronx first pitch, and it went against the plaintiff: Aaron Judge was not added to New York's Wild Card roster. The captain had spent the idle Monday pleading his case in live batting practice — "I've been doing a lot of convincing," he said — but the medical men were not converted. "I don't think he's all the way back," ruled the manager Boone, while calling the progress encouraging; the moderate strain of the right calf's soleus muscle, treated by injection a week ago, ordinarily asks three weeks that the calendar refused to give. The captain's hopes now ride on his teammates: should they pass Boston, the Division Series opens Saturday, and his rehabilitation continues with that date circled — he intends, he has said, to return a full right fielder, not a borrowed bat.

The same roster that closed its door on the captain opened it to two other invalids: Giancarlo Stanton was activated from the sixty-day rolls, and Trent Grisham from the ten-day, the latter patrolling center field before the Game One evening was out. The Herald observes that a 9-0 verdict, entered elsewhere in this number, was obtained without any of the three.

THE HERALD DIPS ITS CAP: HENDRIKS, THE AUSTRALIAN WHO BEAT CANCER BETWEEN SAVES, CALLS IT A CAREER — 'MY ARM HAS TOLD ME IN NO UNCERTAIN TERMS THAT IT HAS EXACTLY ZERO FASTBALLS LEFT IN IT'

Liam Hendriks, seven-and-thirty years of age and fourteen seasons a big-leaguer, announced his retirement Tuesday, and the game is poorer for the quiet. The Australian right-hander leaves a ledger of 490 games and some six hundred sixty-three innings at a 3.88 figure — a 3.16 in relief, where his fame was made: Reliever of the Year in the American League in both 2020 and 2021, thrice an All-Star, and the only man from his continent ever selected more than once. The sternest save of his life was recorded off the field: diagnosed with non-Hodgkin's lymphoma in January of 2023, he took three months of chemotherapy and stood cancer-free by May, Comeback Player of the Year before the season was out, and seven times a nominee for the Clemente award besides. His farewell was in character — no ceremony, only candor: "My arm has told me in no uncertain terms that it has exactly zero fastballs left in it." The Herald submits that the arm gave fair value, and dips its cap to a workingman of the bullpen who never once shorted the till.

THE PURSE DESK: THE NEW MAN POHLAD VOWS THE TWINS WILL 'MEANINGFULLY INVEST' AND CONTEND IN 2027 — THE HERALD ENTERS THE PLEDGE IN PENCIL, THE PAYROLL LEDGER BEING WRITTEN IN INK

In Minnesota, where the faithful have watched an Opening Day payroll of some $153.7 million in 2023 whittled to roughly $109.5 million — two-and-twentieth among the thirty clubs — the franchise's newly designated control man, Tom Pohlad, met the press and made promises. "I understand the patience in this market has run out, and I assure you we have a sense of urgency," said he, vowing the ownership will "meaningfully invest" in the payroll and contend in 2027, though declining to attach a figure to the meaning. The Herald, whose sympathies on matters of the purse are a matter of record, notes that the pledge follows a 77-85 season, a 2025 deadline selloff of uncommon aggression, and three years of the ledger running steadily the other way — and that the ballplayer, unlike the promise, must be paid in currency. The pledge is entered in pencil accordingly; the winter's signings will show whether it deserves ink.

THE RESTING CHAMPIONS: OHTANI PRONOUNCES HIMSELF 'FEELING GREAT' AND WILL SWING STRAIGHT THROUGH THE BYE — FREEMAN SPENDS THE IDLE WEEK IN SEARCH OF THE SWING SEPTEMBER TOOK FROM HIM

From the camp of the hundred-win Dodgers, idle until Saturday's Division Series against the survivor of the Atlanta-Philadelphia quarrel, two bulletins on the state of the machinery. Shohei Ohtani reports himself "feeling great physically" and will continue to hit through the bye week rather than rest the bat — the club expecting him restored to full menace atop the order when the games resume. Freddie Freeman, meanwhile, puts the idle days to humbler use: the eight-time All-Star, whose September was a rough one by his own accounting, is at work rediscovering the swing, professing as ever the power of mind over matter. The Herald notes that clubs which earn the bye are entitled to spend it as they please, and that there are worse omens for the rest of the field than the champions treating a week of rest as a week of work.

The Wednesday tables, then — four contests entered at October's fuller measure, as this paper promised when it retired the summer economy, and the opening night's ledger reads: three hosts held serve, and one guest, the 84-win White Stockings, stole a march in Texas. Tonight the four quarrels resume at the same hours — Philadelphia at Atlanta at two o'clock, the White Stockings at Houston at five, Boston in the Bronx at eight, the Cubs at San Diego at ten — and every one of the four leaders can close its series where it stands, while every trailer plays for the right to see Thursday, when the deciding games would go in the same yards. The trailing clubs may take what comfort history offers, which is little: in four-and-twenty prior series of this best-of-three fashion, but three clubs have lost the opener and lived to advance, and two of those in the spectatorless autumn of 2020. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: Postseason Off-Day Edition — the Nine-and-Twentieth of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 83 · Tuesday, the Nine-and-Twentieth of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the pennant races rest.

0 days until the Wild Card Series Openers (Tuesday, the Nine-and-Twentieth of September).

News Around the League

THE OCTOBER DESK: THE IDLE DAY IS SPENT AND THE WAITING ENDS AT TWO O'CLOCK — FOUR GAME ONES BETWEEN THE MATINEE HOUR AND THE STROKE OF MIDNIGHT, AND EVERY ARM THAT WILL THROW THE FIRST PITCH NOW KNOWN BY NAME

Monday passed exactly as this paper foretold in its last dispatch: not a ball was pitched in anger anywhere in the land, the twelve traveled and talked and took their batting practice behind closed gates, and the only scores kept were at the press conferences. The vigil ends this very day. Four best-of-three series open this afternoon and evening, every game at the higher seed's park, carried on the NBC and Peacock circuits with ESPN Radio crying the action coast to coast.

The card, in order of first pitch, with the duelists now confirmed by the league's own probable-pitcher ledger: Philadelphia at Atlanta at two o'clock at Truist Park, Luzardo (14-5, a 2.86 figure, two hundred one-and-twenty strikeouts) against the grizzled southpaw Sale (14-9, 2.16); the White Sox at Houston at five o'clock at Daikin Park, the rookie Smith (3-3, but a 1.29 figure) against the rookie Blubaugh (5-3, 3.66); Boston at New York at eight o'clock in the Bronx, the rookie Tolle (9-6, 3.03) against Schlittler and his league-best 1.95; and the Cubs at San Diego at ten o'clock at Petco Park, Boyd (10-5, 3.91) against King (12-10, 3.21).

The wage of survival is engraved already: the winners advance to the Division Series opening Saturday, the third of October — Boston's or New York's survivor to Tampa Bay, the Houston series' survivor to Cleveland, the survivor of the San Diego series to Milwaukee, and Philadelphia's or Atlanta's to the hundred-win Dodgers, each at the resting club's yard. Of the four openers the armory desk below gives the particulars, for every one of them carries a story.

THE ARMORY DESK: BOSTON HANDS ITS OPENER TO A MAN YOUNGER THAN ANY SINCE RUTH — COUNSELL SHOWS HIS HAND AT LAST, MATTINGLY SAYS 'START' BUT MEANS 'OPEN,' AND HOUSTON'S DUEL IS A BULLPEN DAY ON BOTH SIDES

The deliberations this paper has chronicled all resolved themselves on the idle Monday, and each resolution repays study. In New York, the manager Tracy passed over his eighteen-game winner Gray and handed Game One to Payton Tolle, three-and-twenty years and three hundred two-and-thirty days of age — the third-youngest man ever to start the first game of a Boston postseason, behind only Smoky Joe Wood of the 1912 World Series and one George Herman Ruth of the 1918. The logic wants no defending: in two starts against these same Yankees the rookie went unbeaten with a 0.69 figure, eighteen strikeouts, and a .093 average against. Opposite him stands Schlittler, who ended Boston's season in last October's Game Three and greets the rematch with relish; Gray takes Game Two.

In Chicago's camp, the hand so long held against the chest — as this paper noted only yesterday — was laid on the table at the eleventh hour: Boyd starts the opener at Petco Park, with Imanaga, Holmes, Peterson, and the sore-shouldered Gausman held in reserve behind him, that last name under the trainers' watch for soreness in the non-throwing shoulder. San Diego answers with its ace King, then likely Pivetta, whose summer was five months lost to a flexor strain. In Philadelphia's camp the word 'start' required amendment: "I should say open," said the interim manager Mattingly of Luzardo, whose whole September amounts to Sunday's four-pitch eighth inning, and whose leash will be short accordingly; Sánchez, fully rested, takes Wednesday's Game Two. And at Daikin Park the afternoon is a bullpen day on both sides of the ledger: Venable's Smith — eight-and-twenty innings of big-league life, and ugly swings induced all the while — opens what his manager plainly calls a bullpen-type game, while Houston counters with Blubaugh as the opener of its own relay, the young man having thrown but fifteen pitches since Friday.

THE CAPTAIN'S CASE: JUDGE PLEADS BEFORE THE ROSTER COURT WITH A CALF THAT WANTS THREE WEEKS AND A CALENDAR THAT GIVES HIM HOURS — 'I'VE BEEN DOING A LOT OF CONVINCING,' SAYS THE MAN, AND THE CONVINCING CONTINUES

The question this paper left open on Monday — whether the Yankee captain's September calf permits him an October — came no nearer its answer on the idle day, though not for want of advocacy. The injury is a moderate strain of the soleus muscle of the right calf, a hurt that ordinarily asks three weeks' healing; the calendar offers considerably less. Judge spent Monday making his case in every available court: four turns at the plate in live batting practice — two walks drawn, a called third strike, a ground ball to the mound — with his running still confined to the anti-gravity treadmill, no stride yet taken on open grass, let alone a cut on the basepaths.

"I've been doing a lot of convincing," said the reigning Most Valuable, "and I'm going to keep doing that." The manager Boone holds the judicial tone — the club prepares as though its captain will not serve, while declining to rule him out; if the medical men give their blessing, the roster has his name on it within the hour. "He's making progress," is as far as Boone will be drawn. The candor of the plaintiff himself deserves entry in the record: "Guys take risks every single day. I understand the risks. I've got it all." The roster is due before this evening's first pitch, and the Herald will report the verdict on the morrow.

THE SPEEDSTER'S DESK: A MAN WHO HAS NEVER PLAYED A BIG-LEAGUE INNING MAY DEBUT IN THE POSTSEASON ITSELF — BOSTON WEIGHS BRAIDEN WARD, HIRED FOR HIS LEGS ALONE, WITH AN OLD 2004 GHOST SMILING ON THE ENTERPRISE

Among the papers Boston must file before tonight's opener is one that would make history of a rare denomination: should the club carry Braiden Ward, the seven-and-twenty-year-old outfielder would become but the seventh man in the game's annals to make his Major League debut in the postseason, and the first of Boston's ever to do so. The résumé is a single sentence long and needs no second: six minor-league seasons, two hundred two-and-seventy stolen bases in five hundred three-and-twenty games, and this summer at Worcester a franchise-record one-and-sixty thefts against nine times caught. He would be carried to do one thing only, and every soul in the park would know the thing, and he would attempt it anyway.

"It's like a dream. It's like a fever dream," said the stringbean — five feet nine, a hundred sixty pounds, and by the beat men's account he talks as fast as he runs. "One day I'm in Worcester, the next day I'm at the nicest hotel I've ever stayed at in New York City with the greatest team, getting to hopefully play in the greatest rivalry." The precedent wants no explaining in that rivalry's precincts: a borrowed pair of legs, a ninth inning in the Bronx, October of 2004 — Roberts stole, Mueller singled, and Boston never lost again. The Herald offers no prophecy, only the observation that history has a weakness for fast men in October.

THE MANAGERIAL DESK: SEATTLE OPENS ITS SEARCH WANTING GRAY HAIRS AND FRESH THOUGHT AT ONCE — AND THE FIRST NAME ON ITS SLATE, THE RUMOR WIRE REPORTS, IS THE VERY MAN WHO ASKED ONLY TO BE WANTED

The vacancy this paper recorded on Monday morning acquired its first candidates by Monday evening. Dipoto, Seattle's baseball chief these eleven years, met the press on the managerial question and set out his specification: unlike Wilson and Servais before him, the next man will have managed in the big leagues — "We need fresh thought," said he, calling for a reset of the culture entire, and adding, with a confidence the 76-86 ledger does not entirely underwrite, that not a candidate in baseball would fail to be excited by the post.

And the first name on the slate, the rumor wire reports through the Seattle Times' account, is one this paper's readers met only yesterday in a San Diego clubhouse doorway: Torey Lovullo, ten years in the Arizona chair, 750-768 with a pennant among the honors, his contract expired and his wish — "I just want to be wanted" — now perhaps to be granted on Puget Sound. Industry men count him among the leading candidates. The remainder of the reported slate runs to Vogt of Cleveland — twice running the American's Manager of the Year, winterer in Olympia, and all but unobtainable, being under contract to a champion; prying him loose would want a trade of the kind not seen since Piniella went to Tampa for an outfielder in 2002 — with Baldelli, Woodward, and Hyde the further names entered. The Herald observes that a man dismissed for finishing 86-76 may yet be hired by a club that finished ten games worse, and that there is a sermon in that somewhere.

THE WAIVER WIRE: ONE SMALL ENTRY ON AN OTHERWISE EMPTY LEDGER — ST. LOUIS CLAIMS THE RIGHT-HANDER HAMPTON FROM WASHINGTON

The transaction column, on a day the whole game held its breath, carried a single line: the Cardinals claimed the right-handed pitcher Chase Hampton off waivers from the Nationals — a winter lottery ticket punched while every other front office in the land was printing October rosters. The Mound City club, its season done these two days, thus fires the offseason's first quiet shot; the Herald enters it in the ledger and moves along to weightier matters.

The Tuesday tables, then — no contests to enter, the pennant races resting one last breath, and the vigil of the idle day kept faithfully to its end. It ends tonight: Philadelphia at Atlanta at two o'clock, the White Sox at Houston at five, Boston in the Bronx at eight, the Cubs at San Diego at ten, four Game Ones stretched from matinee to midnight, and by the small hours the first four verdicts of October will be in. The morrow's dispatch will enter every one of them at October's fuller measure — the summer economy is hereby retired for the season, and each game shall have its full column. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: LEVEL AT SUNRISE, CROWNED BY SUNDOWN — HOUSTON POURS NINE PAST THE WHITE ELEPHANTS WHILE TEXAS FALLS IN MINNEAPOLIS, AND THE WEST'S CROWN COMES HOME AT EXACTLY ONE-AND-EIGHTY WINS: ASTROS 9, ATHLETICS 0
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 82 · Monday, the Eight-and-Twentieth of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 14 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

LEVEL AT SUNRISE, CROWNED BY SUNDOWN — HOUSTON POURS NINE PAST THE WHITE ELEPHANTS WHILE TEXAS FALLS IN MINNEAPOLIS, AND THE WEST'S CROWN COMES HOME AT EXACTLY ONE-AND-EIGHTY WINS: ASTROS 9, ATHLETICS 0

The dead heat this paper has chronicled for a week is settled inside of three innings at West Sacramento — Spence, the taxi-squad thunderbolt, triples home two in a four-run third, Walker thunders his nine-and-twentieth, Alvarez drives home his hundred-sixth on the afternoon his batting crown is sealed, and six Houston pitchers pass a five-hit shutout hand to hand; word arrives from Minneapolis that the Rangers have fallen 6-4, whereupon a club that stood 20-31 in the middle of May is champion of the West at one-and-eighty and one-and-eighty, with the South Siders due at its yard on the morrow

The schedule-maker, a dramatist at heart, had saved the season's last open question for the season's last open afternoon: Houston and Texas level at eighty wins apiece, the American's wild cards all long since spoken for, and the loser of the West — as this paper set out in Sunday's dispatch — to go home outright. Houston declined to let the suspense ripen. By the middle of the third inning at West Sacramento the question was, for all practical purposes, answered.

The third began with small industry — Altuve's groundout cashing Peña, Diaz doubling Alvarez across — and ended with a thunderclap from the least likely quarter: Lucas Spence, the undrafted taxi-squad man whose three-homer Wednesday this paper sang in its Friday columns, lined a two-run triple, the first three-bagger of his big-league life, and it stood 4-0. Christian Walker added his nine-and-twentieth home run in the sixth, Alvarez singled home his hundred-and-sixth run on the very afternoon his .316 average was sealed as the American's batting crown, and the nine ran to a dozen hits. Behind them, six pitchers — Lambert opening, the rookie Pecko taking the decision with three spotless frames, then Ullola, King, VanWey, and Imai — passed the whitewash hand to hand, permitting the Athletics five scattered hits.

In Minneapolis, meanwhile, Texas was breathing its last. Josh Bell struck a two-run blast among three driven home, Royce Lewis added another, and though Corey Seager's two-run answer in the ninth drew the Arlington men to 6-4, no nearer did they come — of which defeat the card below gives the particulars. The wire's obituary was unsparing: the Rangers' season, wrote the Texas correspondent, went out not with a bang but a whimper. And so the ledger closed on one of the strangest championships the divisional age has offered: Houston, champion of the West by a single game, at precisely break-even — one-and-eighty wins, one-and-eighty defeats — the only club of October's twelve without a winning record, and the club that stood twenty wins and one-and-thirty losses in mid-May with Brown, Hader, and Peña all lodged in the infirmary. "Now, we go," ran the word from the Houston clubhouse, and it will serve for a motto.

The wage of the crown — an eighth Western title in the franchise's ledger — is a home date: the South Siders come to Houston Tuesday at five o'clock Eastern to open the Wild Card round, a guest at 84-78 calling upon a host at 81-81. The curiosity this paper mused upon Saturday — an October guest richer in victories than its host — now stands engraved upon the card, and the champions, who took five of seven from Chicago this summer, are invited to prove the standings' arithmetic beside the point.

News Around the League

THE OCTOBER DESK: THE BRACKET IS ENGRAVED ENTIRE — FOUR WILD CARD SERIES OPEN TOMORROW FROM LUNCHEON TO MIDNIGHT, EACH A REMATCH WITH ITS OWN OLD SCORE TO SETTLE

The twelve are known, and the schedule is a banquet: four best-of-three series open Tuesday, every game at the higher seed's park, carried across the NBC and Peacock wires. The card, in order of first pitch: Philadelphia at Atlanta at two o'clock, where the Braves took nine of thirteen meetings this summer but the Phillies have won all three prior October quarrels between the clubs, the ancient left-hander Sale — a 2.16 figure across seven-and-twenty starts, and a career's mastery of Harper and Schwarber besides — waiting to set Atlanta's tone; the South Siders at Houston at five, a rematch of the 2021 October meeting and, for readers of longer memory, of the 2005 World Series itself; Boston at New York at eight, the seventh postseason chapter of the game's oldest quarrel, the Yankees having taken last October's edition two games to one; and the Cubs at San Diego at ten, a rematch of last year's Wild Card round, which Chicago won by the same count — the North Siders having also taken five of six from the Friars this season, one of them by the outlandish score of 23-3.

The four who rest are handsomely rewarded for their summers: Tampa Bay at eight-and-ninety wins and Cleveland in the American, Milwaukee at one hundred three and the Dodgers at one hundred in the National, all idle until the Division Series open Saturday, the third of October, each at home against a Wild Card survivor.

THE ARMORY DESK: NEW YORK HANDS GAME ONE TO SCHLITTLER AND HIS 1.95 — PHILADELPHIA COUNTS ITS SPENT CARTRIDGES, COUNSELL SHOWS NOBODY HIS HAND, AND BOSTON MAY UNCRATE CROCHET

The Yankees settled their deliberations by the simplest of logics: Cam Schlittler, whose 1.95 earned-run average led the American League entire, takes the ball against Boston in Tuesday's opener, with Fried and Cole to follow. The wire desks already speak of the young man as the Cy Young presumptive — this paper reminds its readers that the writers' ballot is not announced until November, and no poll ever threw a strike. The captain Judge, twice an invalid this summer — four-and-eighty games lost to the ribs, then a September calf — declares himself planning to play, though nothing about the leg is certain.

Philadelphia, meanwhile, reaches October counting spent cartridges: Wheeler was pressed into the season's final Sunday and will stand on short rest all series; Sánchez is not fully rested until Wednesday; Luzardo's four-pitch, one-two-three eighth on Sunday was his first work since the seventh of September; and the relief corps carries a 5.79 September figure, the worst in the game. In Chicago's camp, Counsell declines to name so much as a Game One pitcher, preferring, as ever, to hold every card against his chest. And Boston may yet produce a surprise from the crate: the ace Crochet, unseen since the five-and-twentieth of April, threw well in a Saturday session and will likely join the club in New York — as a relief hand, if he is carried at all.

THE CROWNS DESK: THE TABLES CLOSE AND ALONSO TAKES TWO CROWNS IN ONE AUTUMN — A FEAT WITHOUT PRECEDENT IN THE RBI LEDGER, WHILE MORENO NIPS THE HOBBLED ARRAEZ BY A SINGLE POINT

The season's tables are final, and Baltimore's Polar Bear owns the American's summit twice over: Pete Alonso finishes with three-and-forty home runs and one hundred thirteen runs driven in, crowns both — and the runs-batted-in laurel makes him the first man in the game's history to lead each league in that column, having led the National with a hundred thirty-one as a Metropolitan in 2022. Alvarez of Houston takes the American's batting title at .316, with two-and-forty home runs beside; young Simpson of Tampa Bay claims the stolen-base crown at six-and-forty; Gray of Boston leads with eighteen victories; and Schlittler's 1.95, as the armory desk attests, rules the pitching table.

In the National, the batting crown was decided by the width of a hair and a turned ankle: Moreno of Arizona at .311 edges Philadelphia's Arraez at .310 — the race's erstwhile keeper having watched the final days from the invalid list with the sprained ankle this paper has chronicled. The home-run race this paper tracked to the wire ends in a shared crown after all: Crow-Armstrong and Schwarber, locked at five-and-forty apiece since Friday, both went without on the final day, and the two will divide the laurel — though not the October stage, where both appear Tuesday. Burleson of St. Louis takes the National's RBI title at one hundred sixteen, and Nuñez of Washington its stolen-base crown at nine-and-forty.

THE MANAGERIAL DESK: WILSON TAKES HIS LEAVE OF SEATTLE ON THE SEASON'S LAST MORNING — AND IN ARIZONA, LOVULLO, WINNINGEST OF ALL SNAKE SKIPPERS, SAYS ONLY THAT HE WANTS TO BE WANTED

The season's final Sunday claimed its first manager before the first pitch: Dan Wilson gathered his Mariners players and staff in the morning and told them he will not return in 2027, the word reaching the wire through the usual unnamed channels before the club had played out its 76-86 string. The nine, to their credit, sent him off with a 7-3 victory over the Anaheim men, as the card records.

In San Diego's visiting clubhouse, meanwhile, a harder scene: Torey Lovullo, a decade in the Arizona chair and the winningest manager the franchise has known at 750-768, finished out a one-year contract with an eighth October missed in nine years — this one by the width of a weekend, two straight defeats at Petco Park when two victories would have carried the day. Asked whether he wished to return, he said of course; asked whether he would, he could only offer: "I just want to be wanted. I'll leave it at that." The Herald, which watched his club win six straight to force the question to the final afternoon, submits that the man's stock ought to be judged by the chase and not the catch.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: CONTRERAS RETURNS TO BOSTON'S ORDER IN TIME FOR OCTOBER — GASPER AND GUERRERO TAKE HIS PLACE ON THE ROLLS

The ward's ledger balanced itself cruelly in St. Petersburg: Willson Contreras, eight games absent since taking a pitch off the right hand in Texas, returned to Boston's lineup for the finale — hitless in two turns, but the manager Tracy pronounces him ready for the Wild Card round, and his men call the news "huge" for an order that has missed his thunder, .276 and seven-and-twenty home runs' worth before the injury. The corresponding entries are grimmer: Mickey Gasper, whose biceps gave way swinging at a sweeper — a misfortune this paper recorded Saturday — goes formally to the ten-day rolls, and the reliever Tyron Guerrero, his shoulder strained anew after a September already lost to inflammation, to the fifteen-day. Eaton and Olds were recalled to fill the vacancies while the club debates the shape of its October roster.

The Rest of the Card

WHEELER SPENDS HIMSELF GLADLY AND THE COLLAPSE IS CANCELLED AT THE LAST HOUR — FOUR DOUBLES IN TWO INNINGS, TWO LATE THUNDERCLAPS, AND A FIFTH OCTOBER RUNNING: PHILADELPHIAS 7, RAYS 3

The fortnight of agonies this paper has chronicled ended in an afternoon of plenty: Stott, Realmuto, and Schwarber rattled run-scoring doubles to build a 4-0 lead inside two innings, Harper and Sosa added home runs in a three-run fifth, and Wheeler — pressed into the breach on the season's last day — gave six strong innings for his fourteenth victory as Citizens Bank Park exhaled at last. DeLuca homered twice in a gallant Tampa Bay cause; the Rays rest at eight-and-ninety wins and the first seed regardless. Philadelphia banks a fifth consecutive October and travels to Atlanta for Tuesday's opener — and Arizona, whose fate rode on this scoreboard, was thereby dismissed, as the next line tells.

THE DESERT CLAWS LEVEL AND THE FRIARS ANSWER WITH FIVE INSIDE AN INNING — ARIZONA'S SEASON DIES IN THE SEVENTH AT PETCO PARK: FRIARS 9, SONORAN NINE 4

Needing victory and Philadelphia's failure alike, Arizona got neither: down 4-1, the Sonoran nine rallied level in the seventh on doubles and industry — Carroll, Tawa, and Nootbaar each driving home a run — whereupon San Diego answered with five before the frame and its successor were done, Cronenworth walking home the go-ahead run with the bases full and Fermin lining a two-run single toward his three on the night, Hays adding two more in the eighth. The Friars thus close at 91-71, a third consecutive ninety-win campaign built on a 41-18 charge from eleventh place in late July, and will greet the Cubs at ten o'clock Tuesday; the Snakes go home at 86-76, full of honor and empty of October, their manager's melancholy entered at the managerial desk.

BELL'S THUNDER TOLLS THE HOUR AND THE ARLINGTON MEN GO OUT WITH A WHIMPER — SEAGER'S NINTH-INNING PAIR ARRIVES TOO LATE TO MATTER: NORTH STARS 6, ARLINGTON MEN 4

Texas's half of the West's dead heat perished at Target Field: Josh Bell struck a two-run blast among three driven home, Lewis added his fifteenth, and Kremer took the decision while the scoreboard told Houston's tale, the front page giving the full obituary. Corey Seager's two-run twentieth in the ninth, Nimmo aboard, dressed the final line at 6-4 and changed nothing; the Rangers finish 80-82, one game shy of a crown and shut out of October entire, while Minnesota closes a losing year with six wins in its last ten and the small satisfaction of an executioner's steady hand.

A BROKEN FACE, TEN DAYS' REST, AND TWO HOME RUNS — BREGMAN ANNOUNCES HIMSELF FIT FOR OCTOBER AS THE EXILED FINALE PASSES QUIETLY BENEATH THE FLORIDA ROOF: NORTH SIDERS 6, FENWAY MEN 2

The season's strangest fixture — Boston's home finale, played a thousand miles from Fenway under the Tropicana roof to which the nor'easter drove it, as this paper's almanac desk foretold — belonged entirely to Alex Bregman, who in his second game back from the facial fractures a foul ball dealt him struck his seven-and-twentieth and eight-and-twentieth home runs, doubled besides, and drove home four of Chicago's six. Rutschman answered with his thirteenth, and Contreras's return to the order is gladly entered at the ward. The North Siders close at 89-73 and fly for San Diego; the Fenway men, their business at this roofed house long since concluded — they clinched beneath it a week ago — turn for the Bronx.

SEVEN INNINGS, SEVEN STRIKEOUTS, AND PERHAPS A PERIOD — SCHERZER, ON SHORT REST, LEAVES THE LEDGER THREE SHY OF HIS OLD STABLEMATE: MAPLE LEAF NINE 5, QUEEN CITY NINE 1

The vigil this paper promised to keep was rewarded: Max Scherzer, pitching on short rest in what may have been the final start of his life, gave Toronto seven innings of six-hit, one-run baseball and struck out seven — each whiff a stroke against the account, so that the career strikeout ledger this paper reported at ten in Verlander's favor on Sunday now stands at three. Valenzuela's two-run blast and McAdoo's homer and sacrifice fly carried the 5-1 verdict behind him. Only one man may tell Scherzer when it is over, the Toronto correspondent observed, and that man will render no verdict before winter; the Herald holds its edition of the farewell accordingly.

LINDOR RINGS UP THREE HUNDRED AND THE REGISTER OPENS FOR ONLY THE SECOND SWITCH-HITTER OF HIS KIND — THE WASHINGTONS TAKE THE FINALE ANYWAY: WASHINGTONS 6, FLUSHING NINE 4

Thirteen games without a home run ended in the grandest of round numbers: Francisco Lindor's second-inning blast, his one-and-twentieth of the year, was the three-hundredth of his career, making him but the second switch-hitter in the game's annals to join three hundred home runs to two hundred stolen bases. Mauricio homered in the same frame for a 4-1 New York lead, whereupon Washington answered with steady industry — Chaparro homering twice, Abrams tripling home his hundred-and-sixth run — to close its season 6-4 winners, Crews doubling and the young Senators generally auditioning for next April.

MISIOROWSKI TAKES HIS BOW TO A STANDING HOUSE AND THE SUDS MEN BANK ONE HUNDRED THREE — TURANG'S SINGLE IS HIS HUNDREDTH RUN DRIVEN HOME: SUDS MEN 6, MOUND CITY NINE 4

Milwaukee's record-setting summer closed as it was conducted throughout — in front, and in full voice: Jacob Misiorowski, cheered to the mound and cheered from it, took his sixteenth victory against five defeats as the club banked win number one hundred three. Chourio drove home two, Gary Sánchez struck a two-run twelfth, and Brice Turang's first-inning single cashed his hundredth run batted in of the season. St. Louis made it honest late — Bernal's three-run blast in the eighth the freight, Walker reaching one hundred two driven home — but Drohan sealed it, and the first seed now rests until Saturday's Division Series at its own yard.

NINE INNINGS OF STALEMATE, THEN PAGES POURS FOUR THROUGH THE TENTH — THE HUNDREDTH WIN MAKES ROBERTS'S SIXTH SUCH SEASON, A RECORD EQUALLED: DODGERS 5, ORANGE AND BLACK 1

Level at one apiece through nine by the bay, the champions settled matters in the tenth: Call doubled home the go-ahead run and Andy Pages followed with a three-run blast, his three-and-twentieth, for four runs driven in on the night and a 5-1 verdict. The win was the Dodgers' hundredth of the season — and the sixth hundred-win campaign of Dave Roberts's managerial life, equalling the record for the chair. Los Angeles rests until Saturday's Division Series at home; San Francisco closes its books at 65-97, five defeats running.

CONINE'S NINETEENTH HAS THE LAST WORD AND THE FISH CLOSE A WINNING HOUSE — ATLANTA'S TUNE-UP ENDS A HALF-STEP SHORT: FISH 5, BRAVES 3

Miami's farewell was a seesaw won late: Dubón's homer and single had Atlanta ahead and then within one at 4-3 in the seventh, whereupon Griffin Conine's nineteenth restored the two-run margin and Alcantara closed the door. Hernández homered and Serna doubled home two among the Fish's freight; the Marlins thus finish 80-82 — but a stout 47-34 at their own park, where they made a season's habit of inconveniencing their betters. The champions of the East, 94-68 and the National's third seed, lose nothing but tidiness and turn to Tuesday's two o'clock opener against Philadelphia, of which the October desk sings.

PASQUANTINO STRIKES TWICE AND THE SECOND ONE SETTLES IT — THE LAKE ERIE MEN DROP THE FINALE AND LOSE NOT AN INCH: KANSAS CITY NINE 3, LAKE ERIE MEN 2

A finale of pleasant inconsequence for Cleveland turned on Vinnie Pasquantino's bat: the big first baseman homered in the fifth and again in the eighth, the latter breaking a 2-2 knot, while Adell and Schneemann supplied the visitors' answers. Erceg sealed the 3-2 verdict, a parting grace upon Kansas City's 69-93 year. The Lake Erie men rest at 85-77 with the American's second seed and its bye already in the vault, idle until Saturday, when the Division Series opens at Progressive Field against the survivor of the South Siders' errand in Houston.

TWO TWO-RUN THUNDERCLAPS IN A SINGLE THIRD — GRICHUK AND DOYLE SEND THE PALE HOSE TO HOUSTON ON A ROLL: PALE HOSE 4, COLORADANS 2

Chicago's tune-up finished in a single frame: Grichuk and Doyle struck two-run home runs in the third, turning a 1-0 deficit into the whole of the evening's requirement, Kay taking his tenth win and Richards the save while Carrigg's late homer dressed Colorado's line. The Pale Hose close at 84-78 with seven wins in their last ten — the sharpest late form of the American's October class save Cleveland's — and entrain for Houston, where Tuesday's five o'clock opener offers them a division champion owning three fewer victories than themselves. The Coloradans finish 58-104, and are owed a winter's rest.

ON THE MORNING THE MANAGER SAYS FAREWELL, THE EMERALD CITY NINE WIN HIM ONE MORE — AROZARENA'S DOUBLE CAPS A SIX-RUN CUSHION: EMERALD CITY NINE 7, ANAHEIM NINE 3

Hours after Dan Wilson told his men he would not return — the managerial desk gives that account — Seattle played him a proper recessional: three early runs by way of Raleigh's knock and assorted groundwork, then a three-run sixth crowned by Arozarena's two-run double, his four-and-thirtieth two-bagger. Siri's two-run homer off the Anaheim bench's late charge and a Grissom sacrifice fly made the visitors' three; Bazardo took the decision. Two clubs long excused from October thus close at 76-86 and 62-100 respectively, each with an autumn of harder questions than box scores ahead.

THE ROOKIE GRIFFIN OPENS WITH THUNDER AND CLOSES A WINNING YEAR — McGONIGLE AND VALENCIA ANSWER TOO SOFTLY, TOO LATE: CORSAIRS 4, DETROITS 2

Konnor Griffin's first-inning home run, his sixth, set the tone, and his fourth-inning single drove home the last of four Pittsburgh runs — Mangum and Cook supplying the middle freight — as the Corsairs closed their books at 82-80, a winning season banked. Detroit's late answer came from Saturday's heroes: McGonigle's eighteenth and Valencia's eighth, back to back in the seventh — the latter a quieter blow by far than the walk-off thunder this paper sang in Sunday's columns — before Montgomery sealed the 4-2 verdict. The Bengals finish 76-86, their farewell to Verlander already the season's keepsake.

THE ONE LINE LEFT BLANK — THE SEASON'S LAST CARD LOSES ITS BRONX ENTRY, AND ONE HUNDRED SIXTY-ONE GAMES MUST SERVE: ORIOLES AT YANKEES, CANCELLED

The fifteenth fixture of the final day was never played: Baltimore's call at Yankee Stadium was cancelled outright, and with the schedule's book now closed it will not be made up — nothing rode upon it, New York's fourth seed and Tuesday's date with Boston being long since engraved and Baltimore's season long since spent. Both clubs thus close their ledgers at one hundred sixty-one games, a line short of the full complement, the Yankees at 93-68 and the Orioles at 79-82; the scorekeepers will simply rule the page and carry down the totals.

The Monday tables, then — fourteen contests entered, one line ruled blank in the Bronx, and the regular season of 2026 laid to rest entire: every crown assigned, every table closed, and the twelve of October known by name. This day the game rests — the schedule shows not a single contest anywhere in the land — and the combatants travel: Philadelphia to Atlanta for two o'clock tomorrow, the South Siders to Houston for five, Boston to the Bronx for eight, the Cubs to San Diego for ten, all in the best-of-three fashion, while Tampa Bay, Cleveland, Milwaukee, and the Dodgers sharpen their blades for Saturday's Division Series. Tomorrow's dispatch will keep the vigil of the idle day; the one after brings the first October verdicts, whereupon this paper trades its summer economy for October's fuller measure. Until the next dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: FIVE HUNDRED SEVEN-AND-FIFTY STARTS, AND THE LAST ONE ENDS IN TEARS AND THUNDER — VERLANDER SAYS FAREWELL, HIS DAUGHTER RUNS TO THE MOUND, AND VALENCIA WALKS IT OFF: TIGERS 4, PIRATES 3
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 81 · Sunday, the Seven-and-Twentieth of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 13 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

FIVE HUNDRED SEVEN-AND-FIFTY STARTS, AND THE LAST ONE ENDS IN TEARS AND THUNDER — VERLANDER SAYS FAREWELL, HIS DAUGHTER RUNS TO THE MOUND, AND VALENCIA WALKS IT OFF: TIGERS 4, PIRATES 3

Three-and-forty years old, six months removed from a big-league pitch and nursing a hamstring that never quite healed, the old lion gives Detroit five and a third innings and six strikeouts in the valedictory this paper has kept vigil over; seven-year-old Genevieve sprints to the mound as he departs and the man who has seen everything is seen sobbing; whereupon Eduardo Valencia, in the ninth, strikes the two-run blow that turns a 3-2 deficit into a 4-3 triumph, and Comerica Park empties its heart entire

Attend, this paper counseled its readers in Saturday's dispatch, if you stood within a day's ride of Detroit — there would not be another. Those who heeded were paid in full and then in currencies no scorecard has a column for. Justin Verlander, three-and-forty years of age, took a big-league mound for the five hundred seven-and-fiftieth and final time, against Pittsburgh at Comerica Park, and Vintage Verlander answered the bell.

Consider what the afternoon asked of him. He had not thrown a pitch in a Major League game in six months, had not faced an opposing batsman since June, had never fully healed the hamstring that shadowed his summer, and had ramped for this farewell on all of one-and-twenty pitches in a simulated game. The Detroit clubhouse had joked for days about sending him out like Billy Chapel, the celluloid Tiger who closes his career with a perfect game. Perfection was not on offer; nobility was. Five and a third innings, six strikeouts, two runs — a Brandon Lowe home run in the fourth and a Jacob Gonzalez blast in the fifth the only tolls collected — and when the manager Hinch came for the ball, the ambush was sprung: Genevieve, the pitcher's seven-year-old daughter, came sprinting from the wings to seize her father at the mound. "I was totally blindsided, and it hit me like a ton of bricks," said the man who has stared down October unblinking. "I was sobbing." He walked off with his family, which is, on reflection, how a man ought to leave.

The game itself then insisted on matching the occasion. Pittsburgh, its third run supplied by Bryan Reynolds' eighth-inning triple, carried a 3-1 lead into the ninth, and Detroit answered as if scripted: Kevin McGonigle's groundout cashed Max Clark to make it 3-2, and Eduardo Valencia, with Hao-Yu Lee aboard, struck the walk-off blow — his seventh home run, and none will ever be dearer — for a 4-3 verdict, Waguespack collecting the decision. Hollywood, the beat men agreed, would have rejected the draft as too neat.

The ledger closes at five hundred fifty-seven starts and a strikeout account that stands ten clear of one Max Scherzer — of whom the farewell desk below has this very morning's business to report.

News Around the League

THE OCTOBER DESK: THE SEASON'S LAST PAGE IS WRITTEN THIS AFTERNOON — PHILADELPHIA AND ARIZONA SETTLE THE NATIONAL'S LAST BERTH, HOUSTON AND TEXAS SETTLE THE WEST, AND THE LOSER OF THAT LATTER QUARREL GOES HOME OUTRIGHT

Game one hundred sixty-two arrives with two questions still open, and every one of the afternoon's fifteen contests done by suppertime — the whole schedule, fittingly, played in daylight.

The first question is the one this paper has chronicled through a fortnight of Philadelphia agonies: the Phillies, thumped 12-1 by Tampa Bay on Saturday for a fourth consecutive defeat — their bats managing but one unearned run to snap a one-and-twenty-inning scoreless drought — nonetheless still hold the National's final wild card by a single game over Arizona, whose own six-game winning streak was halted in San Diego. The arithmetic is mercifully plain. Philadelphia wins this afternoon against the Rays, with the ace Wheeler taking the ball, and it claims a fifth consecutive October; Philadelphia loses, and it survives only if Arizona also falls at San Diego, the tiebreaker being already in the desert's pocket, as this paper has noted. Lose while Arizona wins, and the Phillies complete what their own scribes are calling the second-worst collapse in the franchise's long and collapse-acquainted history.

The second question is the West's, and it is winner-take-all in the fullest sense: Houston and Texas stand level at eighty wins and one-and-eighty losses, and with all three of the American's wild cards long since spoken for — New York, Boston, and the South Siders — the loser of this race simply goes home. Houston, holding the Silver Boot tiebreaker in its saddlebag still, is champion of the West with a victory at West Sacramento or a Texas defeat in Minnesota; Texas must win and have Houston lose. And when the smoke clears, Tuesday opens the Wild Card rounds: Boston at New York in the Bronx, the Cubs at San Diego by the bay — and the West's new champion entertaining the South Siders.

THE FAREWELL DESK: TEN STRIKEOUTS APART AFTER FORTY YEARS OF SHARED HARNESS — SCHERZER TAKES A TORONTO MOUND THIS AFTERNOON WITH THE LEDGER, AND PERHAPS HIS OWN CAREER, IN THE BALANCE

The game's two great contemporaries have jockeyed for the same laurels since they shared a Detroit rotation from 2010 through '14, and they will not stop merely because one of them has retired. With Verlander's six strikeouts in Saturday's farewell, his all-time account stands precisely ten clear of Max Scherzer on the career leaderboard — and Scherzer, who is not ready to declare his own intentions, takes the mound for Toronto against Cincinnati this very afternoon, knowing it could be his final turn. Between them the two have banked four hundred ninety victories, six thousand six hundred seventeen and a third innings, and six Cy Young Awards; the strikeout ledger is the last account still open. Scherzer, for his part, will render no verdict on retirement until the winter — he means, he says, to see how things unfold. The Herald will keep the vigil it kept for his old stablemate: attend, Toronto, on the chance there is not another.

THE HONORS DESK: A LETTER 'C' IS STITCHED WHERE NONE HAS EVER BEEN — YELICH IS MADE THE FIRST CAPTAIN IN MILWAUKEE'S HISTORY, WITH YOUNT'S BLESSING SOUGHT AND GIVEN FIRST

Before Saturday's 3-2 dispatch of St. Louis, the club with the game's best record did a thing it had never done in its half-century and more: it named Christian Yelich captain and stitched the letter to his jersey. The man's lone condition does him as much credit as the honor: he would not accept until Robin Yount — in Yelich's own reckoning the true first captain, though no letter ever said so — had been asked and had given his wholehearted blessing. "Without his blessing," said Yelich, "I wouldn't have wanted to accept it." Someone in the clubhouse carried the idea to the manager Murphy, who walked it up through the owner Attanasio and the baseball chief Arnold before putting it to Yelich, and thence to Yount. A club sitting on a hundred and two victories has little need of ceremony; it made room for this one anyway, and rightly.

THE MILESTONE DESK: CAMINERO RINGS UP FORTY AND A HUNDRED FOR A SECOND CONSECUTIVE YEAR — AND IN A LOST COLORADO SEASON, GOODMAN STRIKES HIS FORTIETH AND ONE-AND-FORTIETH IN A SINGLE EVENING

Junior Caminero keeps three numbers dear — forty, one hundred, and one hundred sixty-two — and on Saturday in Philadelphia he banked the second of them for the second year running. His first-inning two-run blast off Aaron Nola, home run number two-and-forty, carried him past a hundred runs driven in for the season; the fortieth homer had come on the eleventh of September, on the first walk-off blow of his life, the same swing that clinched Tampa Bay's return to October. "We were looking for another season with 100 RBIs," said the young third baseman. "Thank God we complete it." There remains the third number: he means to start every one of the hundred sixty-two, and this afternoon closes the books.

Colorado's evening in Chicago, meanwhile, produced the season's least-heralded slugging landmark: Hunter Goodman struck his fortieth home run in the third inning and his one-and-fortieth — a three-run affair — in the ninth, a pair of thunderclaps from a club fifty-eight and one hundred three on the year. And atop the American's home-run table, Pete Alonso holds at three-and-forty, the sole proprietor of the crown he seized from a four-way knot on Friday, as this paper recorded, with one afternoon remaining to any challenger.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: TREINEN'S SHOULDER GIVES WAY IN THE BULLPEN AND HIS OCTOBER IS OVER BEFORE IT BEGAN — MIZE JOINS THE INVALID LIST IN SAN DIEGO, AND THE WARD'S EARLIER GUESTS AWAIT THEIR VERDICTS

The cruelest entry of the day required no batted ball at all: Blake Treinen, warming in the Dodger bullpen during Saturday's 4-3 victory by the bay, injured his shoulder in the act of preparing, and the manager Roberts pronounced the season — and thus the postseason — finished for him. "I don't know if it was a complete blowout, but really unfortunate," said Roberts, with imaging to come and the invalid list certain. In San Diego, Casey Mize — whose difficult Friday evening this paper recorded — was placed on the fifteen-day list with a sprained right ankle, Gavin Sheets returning from the invalid rolls in the corresponding move. The ward's earlier admissions hold their beds: Corbin Burnes, shelved Friday with the inflamed shoulder, will seek a second opinion before any next step is chosen, and Luis Arraez's examined ankle — the sprain is pronounced a serious one — leaves his availability for whatever October Philadelphia can still reach very much in doubt.

The Rest of the Card

DOWN THREE IN THE FIRST, THE FOREST CITY NINE ANSWER WITH ELEVEN AND TAKE THE CENTRAL ENTIRE — A THIRD STRAIGHT CROWN, A SEVENTH IN ELEVEN YEARS, AND A BYE BESIDES: GUARDIANS 11, ROYALS 5

Cleveland spotted Kansas City three runs in the first at Kauffman Stadium and then buried the kindness beneath fourteen hits: Patrick Bailey and Brayan Rocchio struck two home runs apiece, DeLauter added his sixteenth, and a four-run ninth sealed an 11-5 verdict — whereupon the White Sox' defeat in Chicago made the clinch official. It is the Central crown for a third consecutive year and the seventh in the last eleven, and with it the American's second seed and the first-round bye, Cleveland resting until Saturday next, the third of October, when the Division Series opens at Progressive Field against the South Siders or the West's survivor. This paper reminds its readers that this club stood one game over the break-even line in early July, minus Ramírez and his mended hand; nine victories in its last ten games is how such a story ends.

SEVENTEEN HITS AND A MILESTONE IN THE FIRST INNING — THE AMERICAN'S BEST TUNE THEIR ENGINES ON PHILADELPHIA'S MISERY: RAYS 12, BROTHERLY LOVE NINE 1

Caminero's two-run first-inning blast off Nola — his two-and-fortieth, and the swing that carried him past a hundred runs driven in, as the milestone desk sings — opened a procession of seventeen hits, Matz taking the decision as Tampa Bay banked victory eight-and-ninety, its fifteenth in one-and-twenty games. For Philadelphia the defeat was a fourth in a row at the cruelest possible hour, and the October desk sets out the arithmetic of the afternoon on which everything now rides.

MACHADO'S THIRTIETH CAPS THE SEEDING QUESTION AND THE SNAKES' STREAK DIES AT SIX — THE MISSION NINE WILL GREET CHICAGO AT HOME TUESDAY: MISSION NINE 10, SNAKES 7

San Diego struck early and often — Machado's three-run thirtieth and Bogaerts' thirteenth the heaviest blows in a thirteen-hit evening — to lock up the National's fourth seed, a third consecutive ninety-win campaign, and a home date when the Wild Card round opens Tuesday at Petco Park — against the very Cubs who ended San Diego's October at Wrigley Field a year ago. Arizona's six-game winning streak perished honorably, a three-run ninth off Mason Miller falling short at 10-7; the visitors' whole season now hangs on this afternoon, as the October desk records.

THE BOTTOM OF THE ORDER CARRIES THE LONE STAR NINE TO THE BRINK OF GAME ONE HUNDRED SIXTY-TWO — FOUR DOUBLES IN A SECOND-INNING BURST KEEP THE WEST ALIVE: LONE STAR NINE 6, MINNESOTANS 2

Shorn of Pederson and Jung, Texas got its rescue from the order's cheap seats: Jansen singled home a run and later homered, and Carter, Osuna, and Nimmo rattled doubles in a four-run second, Eovaldi supplying what his manager called one of the gutsiest starts he has seen before Garcia collected the decision, 6-2. Burger's eight-and-twentieth added the trimming; the wage of the evening is a share of first in the West at eighty wins apiece with Houston, and one afternoon to settle it.

PEÑA STRIKES TWICE, ALVAREZ MATCHES CAMINERO AT TWO-AND-FORTY, AND SPENCE'S LEGEND GROWS — THE HOUSTON NINE ARRIVE AT THE FINAL DAY LEVEL AND ARMED: HOUSTON NINE 13, ATHLETICS 2

A night after spilling six runs through a dropped relay, Houston administered a sixteen-hit correction at West Sacramento: Peña homered twice, Alvarez struck a three-run two-and-fortieth to stand level with Caminero on the American's table, and Lucas Spence — the taxi-squad thunderbolt of whom this paper sang on Friday — doubled and homered besides, Wesneski cruising to the 13-2 decision. The Silver Boot tiebreaker rides with them into this afternoon: win, or watch Texas lose, and the West is Houston's.

GOODMAN'S TWO THUNDERCLAPS GIVE THE MILE HIGH NINE THE LAST WORD OF A LOST SEASON — THE SOUTH SIDERS' TUNE-UP TURNS SOUR IN A FOUR-RUN NINTH: MILE HIGH NINE 9, SOUTH SIDERS 6

Colorado, one hundred three defeats deep and owing nobody anything, played spoiler with relish: Goodman struck his fortieth and — in a four-run ninth — his one-and-fortieth, a three-run blow, while Tovar added his thirteenth in a 9-6 verdict at Rate Field. Chicago's answer of three in the home ninth, Benintendi's fifteenth among it, arrived too late; the defeat cost the wild-card men nothing but tidiness, though it handed Cleveland the Central, as the card's top line attests.

TURANG'S TWO-RUN ANSWER MAKES IT ONE HUNDRED TWO ON THE CAPTAIN'S FIRST DAY — MAY STATES HIS OCTOBER CASE IN THREE HOT INNINGS: MILWAUKEES 3, CARDINALS 2

On the afternoon Yelich took the letter C — the honors desk tells the tale — Milwaukee fell behind on Burleson's six-and-twentieth and answered with Chourio's run-scoring single and Brice Turang's go-ahead two-run blast, his one-and-twentieth, for victory number one hundred two, the relief corps throwing six scoreless behind Dustin May's three striking innings as the club weighs its October rotation. Harrison took the decision over Mathews; St. Louis managed but three hits and made them all count for nearly enough.

HERNÁNDEZ'S NINTH-INNING BLOW SETTLES A SEESAW BY THE BAY — THE BOYS IN BLUE BANK NINE-AND-NINETY WHILE THE WARD CLAIMS TREINEN: BOYS IN BLUE 4, FRISCO NINE 3

Betts' three-and-twentieth had the Dodgers ahead early and San Francisco's two late runs had them level, until Enrique Hernández — October's oldest friend — struck a ninth-inning home run, his fourth, for the 4-3 decision, Scott sealing it. The win was the club's nine-and-ninetieth; its cost, set out at the infirmary ward, was the shoulder of Treinen, injured merely warming to enter.

ONE HIT ONE NIGHT, TEN THE NEXT — THE CROWNED BRAVES RESTORE ORDER AT THE GULF STREAM NINE'S EXPENSE: BRAVES 8, GULF STREAM NINE 3

A night after Eury Pérez silenced them on a single hit — a deed this paper duly sang — the champions of the East remembered themselves: Harris II crossed the plate thrice and doubled a run home, Dominic Smith and Drake Baldwin supplied home runs, and Mederos ran his mark to 6-1 in an 8-3 verdict at loanDepot park. Atlanta enters the season's final afternoon at four-and-ninety wins, the National's third seed.

MAURICIO STRIKES TWICE AND THE METROPOLITANS SPOIL THE SENATORS' SATURDAY — THREE HITS ARE ALL WASHINGTON CAN SHOW FOR NINE INNINGS: METROPOLITANS 7, SENATORS 1

New York's evening turned on a four-run seventh — Ewing's three-run blast, his eleventh, the centerpiece — and Ronny Mauricio homered in the seventh and again in the ninth as the Mets prevailed 7-1, Núñez taking the decision. Washington, held to three hits entire, thus saw its three-game winning streak — the third leg of which this paper recorded only yesterday — expire on the season's next-to-last evening.

BLEDAY'S BLAST AND RODRÍGUEZ'S TRIPLE SEND THE CINCINNATIS HOME WINNERS — TORONTO'S BATS OFFER FIVE HITS TO THE CAUSE: CINCINNATIS 5, JAYS 1

Bleday's four-and-twentieth, Suárez's run-scoring double, and Héctor Rodríguez's two-run triple gave Cincinnati a 5-1 verdict at the Rogers Centre, Lowder besting Yesavage on a night Toronto mustered five hits. The same grounds host weightier business this afternoon: Scherzer takes the Toronto mound against these same Reds, with the farewell desk's ledger — and perhaps a career — in the balance.

THE ANGELS TIE IT WITH SMALL BALL AND THE PUGET SOUND MEN ANSWER WITH THUNDER — CRAWFORD'S TWO-RUN BLOW CAPS A FOUR-RUN SEVENTH: PUGET SOUND MEN 8, ANGELS 4

Two clubs long excused from October staged a lively argument anyway: Los Angeles squared the account at four apiece in the sixth by way of a squeeze bunt and assorted industry, whereupon Seattle poured four across the seventh — Ward's two-run single and J.P. Crawford's fourteenth home run the freight — for an 8-4 verdict, Vargas improving to 3-0. Trout, be it noted, reached second base in the tying rally; the season permits him one more afternoon.

The Sunday tables, then — thirteen contests entered, a farewell wept over in Detroit, and a season that settles its last two arguments this very afternoon, every one of the day's fifteen games played in daylight and done by supper. The stakes, briefly: Philadelphia holds the National's last wild card by one over Arizona — Tampa Bay at Philadelphia at 3:05, Wheeler up; Arizona at San Diego at 3:10 — while Houston and Texas, level at eighty wins, settle the West and the loser's entire October at 3:05 in West Sacramento and 3:10 in Minneapolis respectively, the tiebreaker Houston's. Scherzer, perhaps for the last time, takes the ball in Toronto at 3:07; Boston and the Cubs close the books beneath a Florida roof at 3:05, as this paper recorded Saturday; and Cleveland's newly crowned Central champions play out the string at Kansas City at 3:10 with nothing at hazard but habit. Come Tuesday the Wild Card rounds open — Boston at New York, Chicago at San Diego, and the South Siders at the West's new champion — and this paper trades its summer economy for October's. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.
