entry.title: THE MORNING TAKES THEIR ACE AND THE EVENING ANSWERS WITH ELEVEN — ARIZONA'S SIXTH STRAIGHT DRAWS THE WILD-CARD NOOSE TO A SINGLE GAME: DIAMONDBACKS 11, PADRES 4
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 80 · Saturday, the Six-and-Twentieth of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 17 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THE MORNING TAKES THEIR ACE AND THE EVENING ANSWERS WITH ELEVEN — ARIZONA'S SIXTH STRAIGHT DRAWS THE WILD-CARD NOOSE TO A SINGLE GAME: DIAMONDBACKS 11, PADRES 4

Burnes is sent to the invalid list at midday, his shoulder inflamed, on the very eve of his appointed start; whereupon Nootbaar strikes the night's first blow with a home run, Perdomo triples and doubles and drives home four, Arenado strikes his thirtieth and Lawlar his sixth, and Mize is chased beneath seven runs in four innings, Pfaadt carrying the verdict into the eighth — and Philadelphia having been blanked at home by Tampa Bay the selfsame evening, the Phillies' hold on the National's last wild card stands at one game with two to play, the tiebreaker already in Arizona's pocket

The day dealt Arizona its blow before luncheon. Corbin Burnes, fifteen months rebuilt from elbow surgery and but three starts into his return, was placed on the fifteen-day invalid list with an inflamed shoulder — this on the very eve of the start appointed him, with the club's whole October riding on the weekend. A nine six victories deep in a streak might have read the omen and shuddered; the men from the desert elected instead to render the question of Saturday's pitcher nearly academic, and Jose Cabrera was summoned up from Reno to fill the roster's hole while the lineup went about filling the scorebook.

Lars Nootbaar struck the night's first blow, depositing an early Casey Mize offering in the right-center seats before the first inning was minutes old. By that frame's close, Perdomo had tripled a run home and Carroll had lifted a sacrifice fly; before Mize escaped the fourth — he did not, in truth, escape it — the sidewinders had struck him for seven runs on seven hits, three of them home runs: Nootbaar's eighth, Arenado's thirtieth, Lawlar's sixth. Perdomo finished with four runs driven in, and Brandon Pfaadt, handed riches, carried the ball into the eighth inning of an 11-4 verdict before a packed house at Petco Park, whose home club — its berth long since secured — let slip its chance to seal the fourth seed and now hears Chicago's spikes a game and a half behind.

The arithmetic is the story, and it is written in two cities. In Philadelphia the same evening, the Phillies were whitewashed by Tampa Bay, 2-0 — their twelfth blanking of the year and third straight defeat — and so the lead Arizona has chased since it stood six games and a half on the first of September is now a single game, with two to play. The tiebreaker, be it noted, is already Arizona's: the clubs split their six meetings and the next criterion fell to the desert, so a dead heat at season's end sends the Phillies home. Philadelphia still holds the pen — any combination of Phillie victories and Arizona defeats summing to two closes the book — but the club that could not lose a week ago now cannot stop winning, six straight since a Friday defeat in the Bronx, and its clubhouse speaks of something magical riding with them.

The clinch this paper saw within Philadelphia's reach on Wednesday remains unsigned four days later, and the ghosts of 1964 are being spoken of aloud in that city. Tonight the sidewinders try San Diego again, Buehler taking the ball for the Friars, while Philadelphia gets Tampa Bay once more — and every scoreboard in two time zones will be read twice.

News Around the League

THE OCTOBER DESK: CLEVELAND AND CHICAGO BOTH WIN AND THE CENTRAL STAYS ONE GAME APART WITH A BYE FOR THE TAKING — THE WEST'S DEAD HEAT SURVIVES BY MUTUAL FAILURE, AND THE BRONX PREPARES FOR BOSTON

Two days remain, and the American's two open questions each held their ground. In the Central, Cleveland and Chicago both banked victories — the Guardians untidily, the White Sox emphatically — and so the Guardians' lead stands at one game, with the tiebreaker in Chicago's keeping, as this paper has noted, meaning Cleveland must finish a game clear or yield the crown. The stakes are handsomer than a pennant flag alone: the Central's winner is assured the American's second seed and its first-round bye, the West's champion being unable to better one-and-eighty wins, while the Central's loser — though richer in victories than the West's champion by any arithmetic — must travel as the sixth seed to that very champion's yard when the Wild Card rounds open Tuesday. A guest with more wins than its host: October has staged stranger things, but not many.

In the West, the dead heat survived a fourth consecutive night, this time by mutual failure: Houston spilled six runs through a dropped relay in the sixth at West Sacramento, Texas was thumped by ten in Minnesota, and the co-tenants of the throne remain nine-and-seventy wins apiece — each, remarkably, two games under the break-even line — with the Silver Boot tiebreaker still in Houston's keeping. Win its last two and Houston is champion of the West, whatever Texas does.

The one October pairing already engraved: New York and Boston, the wild card's first and second seeds, will open at Yankee Stadium on Tuesday — the seventh postseason meeting of the game's oldest quarrel. In the National, the last berth is the front page above; the remaining suspense is seeding, where San Diego's defeat and Chicago's twin setbacks leave the Cubs a game and a half behind the Friars for the top wild card, with the Cubs holding but a single game to play.

THE MILESTONE DESK: DE LA CRUZ STEALS HIS WAY INTO CINCINNATI'S THIRTY-THIRTY REGISTRY — ALONSO BREAKS THE FOUR-WAY TIE AT THE AMERICAN'S SUMMIT, AND A RECORD NOBODY COVETS FALLS ON THE SOUTH SIDE

Elly De La Cruz doubled home two in Toronto, then stole third on the very next pitch — his thirtieth theft, joined to thirty home runs, making him only the fourth Red in the franchise's long history to post a thirty-thirty season, after Eric Davis, Barry Larkin, and Brandon Phillips. Nine of his home runs have come in September alone; the club's evening ended 6-5 the wrong way, but the register does not care.

The American's home-run crown, a four-way knot at one-and-forty when this paper recorded it in Thursday's dispatch, is a knot no longer: Pete Alonso struck twice in the Bronx matinee and stands alone at three-and-forty, two clear of Alvarez, Caminero, and Rice with two mornings left. In the National, Crow-Armstrong and Schwarber remain locked at five-and-forty apiece — though the Cub has but one game remaining to the Phillie's two.

And on the South Side, a record was set that no man ever campaigned for: Colson Montgomery struck out for the two-hundred-four-and-twentieth time this season, the most whiffs any batsman has recorded in a single campaign since the game began counting. The Herald notes, in fairness to the young man, that his club is bound for October and he has swung hard the whole way there.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: JUNG'S HAND IS BROKEN IN ARLINGTON'S DARKEST HOUR — GASPER'S BICEPS LIKELY COSTS HIM OCTOBER, AND ARRAEZ'S PICTURES COME BACK UNKIND

The ward filled cruelly on the season's next-to-last Friday. In Minnesota, Texas lost more than a game: Josh Jung took a four-and-ninety-mile fastball from Joe Ryan off the right hand, stayed in long enough to score, and learned afterward the hand is fractured. "Devastated — period," said the man himself. He had batted .341 since returning from the invalid list a fortnight ago, and the Rangers' ledger reads 53-50 with him in the order, 26-30 without.

In Boston, Mickey Gasper — whose late-season thunder this paper saluted but three days past — wrenched his right biceps merely swinging through a sweeper in the matinee, and his manager pronounced the injury significant and likely to take him from the October roster. The ripples reach the whole batting order: Duran to left field against the right-handers, Anthony to the designated place.

And in Philadelphia, where no bad news travels alone, the batting title's keeper got his pictures back: Luis Arraez's sprained left ankle, turned dodging a tag on Thursday, drew from interim manager Don Mattingly the grim verdict "kind of not a great one." His availability for the final games — and for the postseason the Phillies are still trying to reach — is very much in doubt.

THE HERALD LOWERS ITS COLORS: BILL GILES, WHO GAVE PHILADELPHIA HALF A CENTURY, PETE ROSE, AND THE PHANATIC, IS DEAD AT TWO-AND-NINETY

William Giles, son of the National League president Warren Giles and for more than fifty years the animating spirit of the Philadelphia club, died Friday at his home in Gladwyne, Pennsylvania, at the age of two-and-ninety. He came to the Phillies in 1969 to mind the business side and ended by owning a piece of the whole enterprise, organizing the syndicate that bought the club from the Carpenter family in 1981 and serving as president and chief executive until 1997, chairman thereafter, and chairman emeritus to the last. It was Giles who persuaded Ruly Carpenter to sign Pete Rose for the club that won it all in 1980, Giles who helped conjure the Phillie Phanatic into green and permanent existence, and Giles whom the National League made its honorary president in 2001. Citizens Bank Park stood for a moment of silence before Friday's game. The Herald lowers its colors for a man who understood that the game is also a show, and made the show worthy of the game.

THE ALMANAC DESK: THE NOR'EASTER WINS ITS SERIES WITH BOSTON — THE SEASON'S FINAL GAME REMOVES TO A FLORIDA ROOF, AND THIS AFTERNOON BELONGS TO VERLANDER AT THE PARK WHERE IT ALL BEGAN

The storm this paper flagged in Friday's dispatch has now redrawn the schedule entire. Having already forced Friday's twin bill, the nor'easter bearing down on New England has driven the Red Sox and Cubs clean out of Boston: the league has ordered their season finale played Sunday afternoon at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, the clubs flying south Friday night to idle through Saturday under clearer skies. The Cubs' objection to a hasty Saturday date — "they never move games up... within a five-day window of a starting rotation," manager Craig Counsell had protested — was accommodated, and so the 2026 season will close, for two northern clubs, beneath a Florida roof.

And this afternoon at ten minutes past one, at Comerica Park in Detroit, Justin Verlander takes a big-league mound for the final time, against Pittsburgh — the valedictory this paper has kept vigil over since it was named. The regular season's last day is tomorrow, the six-and-twentieth being its next-to-last; the Wild Card rounds open Tuesday, the nine-and-twentieth. Attend today's game if you are within a day's ride of Detroit, reader. There will not be another.

The Rest of the Card

ANTHONY STRIKES THRICE AND THE MATINEE GOES TO THE BOSTONS — TWO CUBS CROSS THE PLATE IN ONE SCRAMBLE AND STILL THE OPENER IS LOST: BOSTONS 4, CUBS 3

The twin bill played to outrun the weather opened with Roman Anthony reaching base four times, hitting safely thrice, and scoring thrice, two doubles and a triple among his afternoon's work, while Rutschman drove home two of Boston's four. Chicago's third run arrived by way of a curiosity — Busch and Swanson sliding across the plate in the same instant on Amaya's knock, a photograph's worth of tangled Cubs — but the visitors got no nearer; Weissert took the decision and Burgos sealed it. Gasper's fifth-inning departure is entered, grimly, at the ward.

THE NIGHTCAP IS A WHITEWASH AND FENWAY'S HOME SEASON CLOSES ON A SWEEP — ABREU'S DOUBLE CASHES BOTH RUNS: RED SOX 2, CUBS 0

The evening game needed only Wilyer Abreu's two-run double, his eight-and-thirtieth two-bagger of the year, and four hits total to finish the sweep — Chicago out-hit Boston seven to four and scored nothing for it, Paez taking his first victory of the campaign. So ends regular-season baseball at Fenway Park for 2026, on the highest of notes for the home nine; the two clubs' actual finale rides south to St. Petersburg, as the almanac desk records, and the Cubs limp toward it having dropped a game and a half behind San Diego for the top wild card.

BEAVERS DRIVES HOME FOUR AND ALONSO STRIKES TWICE TO STAND ALONE ATOP THE AMERICAN — THE O'S SPOIL THE BRONX MATINEE ENTIRE: ORIOLES 10, YANKEES 2

Baltimore's afternoon was a thirteen-hit procession: Beavers homered and drove in four, Jackson added a blast of his own, and Pete Alonso struck his two-and-fortieth and three-and-fortieth of the season — three runs driven home, and sole possession of the American's home-run lead, as the milestone desk attests. Suárez took the win against Beck, and the champagne-tested Yankees looked, for an afternoon, like a club with its trunk already packed.

WARREN RESTORES ORDER BY NIGHTFALL AND THE HIGHLANDERS TAKE THE NIGHTCAP — VOLPE'S PAIR SETTLES THE SPLIT: HIGHLANDERS 6, ORIOLES 3

The nightcap belonged to Will Warren, eleven victories now against six defeats, whose commanding turn read like an audition for October work; Volpe drove home two and Rice, McMahon, and the rest chipped in doubles enough for a 6-3 verdict and a split of the day. Beavers homered again for Baltimore — his ninth, his second of the day — a footnote of persistence in a lost season. New York's eye is already on Tuesday, when Boston comes to the Bronx for the two rivals' seventh meeting of an October.

TEN STRIKEOUTS BUY SÁNCHEZ NOTHING AND THE TAMPA MEN PASS THE WHITEWASH HAND TO HAND — PHILADELPHIA'S TWELFTH BLANKING FALLS AT THE CRUELEST HOUR: TAMPA MEN 2, PHILLIES 0

Cristopher Sánchez gave the Phillies seven innings and ten strikeouts and was beaten anyway, his record falling to 18-7 on a first-inning single by DeLuca and Fortes' sixth home run in the second. Freddy Peralta answered with five and a third scoreless frames and four relief hands passed the shutout to Baker, whose one-and-fortieth save banked Tampa Bay's seven-and-ninetieth win. Forty thousand at Citizens Bank Park — having stood in silence for Bill Giles before the first pitch — spent the later innings booing the home nine, whose predicament the front page sets out in full. Harper singled and clapped toward his dugout in the sixth; whether encouragement or desperation, the town could not say.

TORKELSON'S THUNDER, AND A TRIPLE BESIDE — THE BENGALS OUTLAST SEVEN PITTSBURGH RUNS ON THE EVE OF THE FAREWELL: BENGALS 8, SMOKY CITY NINE 7

Spencer Torkelson supplied a home run, his six-and-twentieth, a triple, and three runs driven in, and Dingler added two more as Detroit survived a seven-run Pittsburgh evening — Flores Jr. homering and driving in three among the visitors' answering fire. Jobe took the decision and the ancient Jansen recorded his two-and-twentieth save, tidying the stage for this afternoon, when Verlander gives Comerica its valediction.

CREWS STEALS TWO AND HOMERS BESIDES — THE CAPITAL NINE MAKE IT THREE STRAIGHT AT THE METS' EXPENSE: CAPITAL NINE 7, METS 6

Dylan Crews homered, stole two bases, and generally conducted himself like a man auditioning for next April, while Abrams drove home two to reach a hundred and five on the season as Washington took its third in a row, 7-6. Bichette homered and drove in a pair and Benge struck his twentieth for New York, whose season now has one page left; Varland won it and Gray closed it — the latter's first save of the year.

OKAMOTO DRIVES HOME THREE AND TORONTO SHADES A SEESAW — DE LA CRUZ'S MILESTONE EVENING GOES UNREWARDED: TORONTOS 6, REDS 5

Okamoto's three runs driven in tipped a back-and-forth affair at the Rogers Centre, Fluharty improving to 7-1 and Varland banking his five-and-thirtieth save. For Cincinnati, De La Cruz doubled home two and stole his way into the thirty-thirty registry — the milestone desk gives the honor its due — and Suárez struck his six-and-twentieth, but five runs on twelve hits proved one short of six on ten.

NINE INNINGS, ONE HIT, NOT A RUN — EURY PÉREZ WALKS THE WHOLE ROAD ALONE AND ATLANTA IS SILENCED ENTIRE: MIAMI NINE 3, BRAVES 0

The deed of the night that decided nothing and deserves everything: Eury Pérez went the distance at loanDepot park and permitted the champions of the East precisely one hit — nine innings, one walk, eight strikeouts, nine-and-twenty men faced, a hundred and five pitches, and the whole business transacted in two hours and one minute flat. Mack and Conine supplied home runs, Hernández singled home Marsee, and the crowned Braves, whatever they were resting for, were made to look mortal in the meantime. The Herald's masthead promises no deed unsung; consider this one sung.

THREE LEADS SQUANDERED, THEN FIVE RUNS ON SIX WALKS IN THE NINTH — CLEVELAND'S UGLIEST VICTORY MAY PROVE ITS DEAREST: GUARDIANS 12, ROYALS 9

No painter will hang it, but the ledger accepts all styles: Cleveland blew three separate leads at Kauffman Stadium before mounting a five-run ninth built chiefly of six bases on balls, three of them forcing runners home, to escape 12-9 and keep its one-game hold on the Central. Martínez drove home four and Ramírez two — the latter also committing two errors, in the spirit of the evening — while Kansas City's Jensen homered twice and drove in five in a gallant losing cause. "We have no idea how we're going to find a way to win," allowed manager Vogt, "but we're going to continue to try to find a way to win every night." With the bye riding on it, the Herald recommends he keep trying.

MURAKAMI STRIKES TWICE AGAINST HIS OLD TOKYO ADVERSARY — CHICAGO'S ANSWER TO CLEVELAND ARRIVES INSIDE THE HOUR: WHITE SOX 6, ROCKIES 1

Munetaka Murakami greeted Tomoyuki Sugano — his old adversary from the Japanese leagues, and once his World Baseball Classic teammate — with two home runs, his four-and-thirtieth and five-and-thirtieth, driving in three before the tenth sellout crowd of the season at Rate Field, 35,778 strong. He had twice homered off Sugano in Japan; some correspondences survive an ocean. Burke took his eleventh win, Teel drove home two, and the White Sox — showing, in the words of their own beat man, no celebration hangover whatever — kept their deficit at one game with two to play.

TURANG DRIVES HOME THREE AND THE HUNDRED-AND-FIRST IS BANKED — THE BREW CREW TUNE FOR OCTOBER AT ST. LOUIS'S EXPENSE: BREW CREW 8, GAS HOUSE NINE 4

Milwaukee's machine, first seed long since pocketed, added a hundred-and-first victory for the shelf: Turang doubled twice and drove home three to reach seven-and-ninety runs batted in, and Bauers added a pair. St. Louis supplied thunder without consequence — Herrera, Walker, and Burleson all homered, the last's two runs driven in stretching his National-best ledger to a hundred and fifteen — but Uribe and the relief corps held the line from there.

KEASCHALL EVERYWHERE, AND deGROM'S LAST REGULAR TURN GOES AWRY — TEXAS'S HALF OF THE THRONE TAKES A TEN-RUN BEATING: TWIN CITIES NINE 10, RANGERS 2

On the night Texas could least afford it, Minnesota administered a 10-2 thrashing: Keaschall doubled, tripled, stole a base, and drove home three, Clemens struck his seven-and-twentieth with three runs batted in besides, and Joe Ryan took the decision. Jacob deGrom, making the final regular-season start of his campaign, absorbed the loss — and the evening's true cost was dearer still, Jung's broken hand being entered at the ward. Texas remains level with Houston atop the West only because Houston lost too.

ALTUVE DROPS THE RELAY AND SIX SPILL THROUGH THE SIXTH — THE ATHLETICS PLAY SPOILER AND THE WEST'S KNOT HOLDS: ATHLETICS 6, ASTROS 5

Houston's hundred-and-sixtieth game turned on a single dropped ball: with none out in the sixth at West Sacramento, Altuve let Peña's relay fall from his glove at second base, a double play dissolved into nothing, and the Athletics poured six runs through the opened door. Walker's eight-and-twentieth and Smith's one-and-twentieth kept the visitors close, and a late rally fell one short against Harris's save. "Really bad," said Altuve of the drop. "Not a good feeling." The consolations are two: Texas lost as well, and the Silver Boot tiebreaker still rides in Houston's saddlebag — win the last two, and the West belongs to the Astros outright.

NETO'S SEVEN-AND-TWENTIETH AND MOORE'S THREE DRIVEN HOME — THE HALOS PLAY OUT THE STRING WITH SPIRIT BY THE SOUND: HALOS 7, MARINERS 5

Two clubs long since excused from October played anyway, as the schedule insists: Zach Neto doubled twice, homered, and stole a base, Moore drove home three, and Detmers — whose two hundred eleven strikeouts stand fourth in the American — took the win. Canzone's three-and-twentieth and Arozarena's triple kept Seattle in it to the end; the end came regardless, 7-5.

SKUBAL'S SEVEN SPOTLESS AND TEN STRUCK OUT — TWO SECOND-INNING THUNDERCLAPS ARE ALL THE CHAMPIONS REQUIRE BY THE BAY: DODGERS 2, BAY NINE 0

Tarik Skubal's regular season closed like a vault door: seven innings, three hits, not a walk, ten strikeouts, and the Giants dismissed 2-0 on Hernández's and Pages' second-inning home runs off Marte. Behind him the October machinery clicked once in rehearsal — Sasaki with a perfect eighth for his first hold, Scott with a perfect ninth for his four-and-twentieth save — and the champions banked win eight-and-ninety with their rotation's edge gleaming.

The Saturday tables, then — seventeen contests entered, two of them twin bills played against the weather, and every race alive into the season's final two days. In the American: Tampa Bay holds the first seed at seven-and-ninety wins; New York and Boston are engraved for Tuesday in the Bronx; Cleveland leads Chicago by one for the Central and its bye, the tiebreaker Chicago's — Cleveland plays tonight at Kansas City at 7:10, Colorado visits the South Side at the same hour — and the West is a dead heat at nine-and-seventy wins, Houston at the Athletics and the Angels at Seattle at 9:40, Texas at Minnesota at 4:10. In the National: Milwaukee sits on a hundred and one wins and the first seed; Philadelphia's lead over Arizona for the last wild card is one game, Tampa Bay at Philadelphia at 7:15 and Arizona at San Diego at 8:40 tonight; San Diego leads Chicago by a game and a half for the top wild card. The day's other cards: the Mets at Washington; Pittsburgh at Detroit at 1:10, where Verlander says his farewell; Cincinnati at Toronto at 3:07; the champions at San Francisco at 4:05; Atlanta at Miami at 4:10; St. Louis at Milwaukee at 7:10. Tomorrow is the season's last page — one line of it to be written, of all places, under a Florida roof. Until the next dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: SIXTEEN GAMES A BIG-LEAGUER AND THREE HOME RUNS IN A NIGHT — EVERY BLOW OF LUCAS SPENCE'S LIFE ARRIVES AT ONCE, AND HOUSTON'S HALF OF THE THRONE HOLDS: ASTROS 7, ATHLETICS 5
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 79 · Friday, the Five-and-Twentieth of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 12 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

SIXTEEN GAMES A BIG-LEAGUER AND THREE HOME RUNS IN A NIGHT — EVERY BLOW OF LUCAS SPENCE'S LIFE ARRIVES AT ONCE, AND HOUSTON'S HALF OF THE THRONE HOLDS: ASTROS 7, ATHLETICS 5

A rookie summoned from the taxi squad but two days prior — undrafted out of a school few atlases bother with, hitless the night before — strikes the first three home runs of his career in a single evening at West Sacramento: a three-run blow in the second, the tie-breaker in the seventh, and a first-pitch exclamation to open the ninth, five runs driven in entire; only the third man in the game's long history whose first three came at once; and with Texas victorious that afternoon, the blows keep the West's dead heat alive at nine-and-seventy wins apiece with three to play, the tiebreaker still Houston's

Until Wednesday, Lucas Spence was a name on the Houston taxi squad — an undrafted free agent of 2024 out of Southern Illinois-Edwardsville, owner of twelve home runs this season split between Sugar Land and Corpus Christi, summoned only because Varsho's wrist gave out. On Wednesday night in Seattle he went hitless in three trips with two strikeouts, late on every fastball he saw. On Thursday he sat with his coaches, moved his hands, found his timing — and then, in the sixteenth big-league game of his life, hit three home runs, drove in five, and may have saved Houston's season.

The first was a three-run blow off the starter Barnett in the second inning, a ball sent 429 feet by the measuring instruments with Walker and Smith aboard: three to nothing. The Athletics answered with four in the third — McNeil's three-run homer and the first of Zack Gelof's two — and there the game hung, four-to-three against, until Paredes squared it with his four-and-twentieth in the sixth. Whereupon the rookie struck again: a solo blow off the reliever Blewett in the seventh for the lead, five-to-four. Walker's seven-and-twentieth made it six in the eighth, Gelof answered once more, and Spence, leading off the ninth, swung at the first pitch he saw from Alvarado and deposited it in the right-field seats. Three home runs, numbered one, two, and three of a career. The registry holds only two other men whose first three arrived in a single game — Zavala of the 2021 White Sox, and the Cardinals' Báez, who managed it in his very debut this August — and now Spence of the 2026 Astros, in a game his club could not afford to lose. "It was really shocking, to be honest," the young man offered. "Just really trying to get base hits, but sometimes you run into a couple of homers." The beaten manager Kotsay put it plainer: "We ran into a hitter tonight that had a career night, and that happens in this game sometimes."

The bullpen, mindful of history even as the rookie Ullola and the closer Abreu were sealing the victory, mounted a salvage operation for the evidence: the bullpen catcher Bracamonte bartered batting gloves and a signed ball to a boy in the stands for the first ball, Abreu near caught the second on the fly, and the third was thrown back to the relief corps by the Athletics' own right fielder Butler — three baseballs bound for a mantel in Edwardsville. The arithmetic they decorate is entered at the October desk: Texas had won that afternoon, so Houston's victory keeps the West a dead heat at nine-and-seventy wins apiece with three to play, the Astros closing at these same Athletics with the Silver Boot tiebreaker still in their keeping. "I enjoy watching young players come up here on the biggest stage there is," said the manager Espada. "We needed some of those kids to step up and do big things, and he just delivered." Yesterday they threw fastballs past him; today his name is in the registry. The pennant races make heroes on short notice.

News Around the League

THE OCTOBER DESK: FOUR CLINCHES BETWEEN LUNCHEON AND MIDNIGHT — THE SOUTH SIDE, CLEVELAND, THE NORTH SIDE, AND SAN DIEGO ALL TAKE THEIR CHAIRS, MILWAUKEE POCKETS THE FIRST SEED ENTIRE, AND THREE RACES RIDE INTO THE WEEKEND

Thursday was the calendar's great day of settling: four clubs clinched their October places between the afternoon and the midnight wires, and the postseason field now wants only the answers to three questions. The White Sox seated themselves first, by nine-to-one at Kansas City — the South Side's first October since it won the Central of 2021, and a resurrection from three consecutive seasons of a hundred defeats, among them the modern record of one-and-twenty-and-a-hundred in 2024. "They have belief in themselves, belief in each other," said the manager Venable. "That can carry you a long way." Cleveland followed within the hour, its one-nothing verdict at Fenway clinching a third consecutive berth and the nineteenth in the franchise book — "This is why we play," said the manager Vogt. "We play to give them an October to remember." By afternoon's end at Wrigley the Cubs had punched their own ticket, a second consecutive October for the first time since the four-year run of 2015 through '18; and by night the Padres had beaten the champions at Los Angeles to bank a third straight autumn for the first time in franchise history, the fifth berth in seven years. That same defeat handed Milwaukee the National's first seed entire — the Brewers, at a hundred wins, now hold home ground for as long as their October lasts, as the card below relates.

The three questions, then. In the American's Central, Cleveland leads Chicago by one with three to play, and the tiebreaker is Chicago's — the Guardians must finish plainly ahead, their closing three at Kansas City while the White Sox host Colorado; the division's winner takes the bye-less third seed and the loser drops to the wild-card row's last chair. In the West, the dead heat holds at nine-and-seventy wins apiece — Houston hosts nothing and travels nowhere, closing its three at the Athletics, while Texas opens three at Minnesota tonight — and Houston's tiebreaker still governs: win alongside the Rangers each day, and the division is Houston's; the loser of this race goes home entirely, and the winner may yet wear a crown with a losing ledger, a curiosity the game has rarely bothered to permit. In the National, one chair remains: Philadelphia, twice beaten running, holds the last wild card by two games over an Arizona club riding five straight victories — the Quakers host Tampa Bay needing to close the account by their own hand, while the Desert nine, whose twelve-run Thursday is on the card, must take at least two of three at San Diego and pray the Sunshine nine do them a service besides.

THE MILESTONE DESK: A STOLEN BASE IN THE FIRST INNING OF A CLINCHER — CROW-ARMSTRONG BECOMES THE SEVENTH MAN OF THE FORTY-FORTY REGISTRY, AND SKENES BANKS TWO HUNDRED STRIKEOUTS A SECOND YEAR RUNNING

Pete Crow-Armstrong walked to open the first inning of the Cubs' clinching afternoon, and was running on the very next pitch — sliding into second before the Miami infield had fairly considered the matter, and into the registry with the theft: forty home runs and forty stolen bases in a single season, the seventh man in the game's history to hold both figures at once and the first Cub ever. The company he joins wants no introduction — Ohtani, Acuña, Soriano, Rodriguez, Bonds, and Canseco — and the Wrigley faithful, who have chanted his initials since his debut, have lately amended the cry to three different letters. "I wanted to put myself in that same conversation as such impressive and great players," said the center fielder, whose five-and-forty home runs share the National's lead besides, "but every day I showed up like, if I took the right base, it was going to help the team." His manager Counsell reckons the season one for the grandchildren's hearing; the operations chief Hoyer settled for the ledger: "There are only so many guys in the game that can even think about accomplishing it."

At Pittsburgh the same afternoon, Paul Skenes struck out his two-hundredth batsman of the year in the Bucs' two-to-one decision over St. Louis — the second consecutive season the young right-hander has reached the figure, and a milestone banked in a game his bullpen finished for him, as the card relates. The pitching ledgers thus close their season's accounts one by one: Misiorowski of the hundred-win Brewers holds the National's strikeout lead at seven-and-forty-and-two-hundred, with Skenes among the four men knotted at an even two hundred behind him.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: THE BATTING TITLE'S KEEPER TURNS AN ANKLE DODGING A TAG — ARRAEZ'S PICTURES ARE CLEAN BUT THE WEEKEND UNCERTAIN, CONTRERAS CANNOT YET SWING FOR BOSTON, AND A WRIST IN HOUSTON OPENED A ROOKIE'S DOOR

The National's batting race may have been decided by an umpire's judgment call. Luis Arraez, whose .310 figure leads the league by two points over Arizona's Moreno, rolled his left ankle in the sixth inning at Philadelphia on Thursday — dodging a tag after a wide throw pulled the first baseman off the bag, only to be ruled out of the baseline for his trouble. He left the field on a trainer's arm, shouting his innocence at the plate umpire from the dugout; the hitting coach Long was ejected for seconding the motion; the X-rays came back negative, a sprain and nothing worse. "I'm hopeful that he can play," said the interim manager Mattingly, "but we'll see" — and with the wild card unclinched and the Wild Card round opening Tuesday, the Quakers can ill afford the subtraction. "That would be rough," the shortstop Turner agreed.

At Boston the news ran no kinder. Willson Contreras, the first baseman whose seven-and-twenty home runs anchor the Crimson Hose order, has not swung a bat in two days — the knuckle he took a pitch upon a week ago still too swollen to grip through. "I mean, it's really concerning," he owned Thursday night, near tears at his locker. "We play to play in October, and it's really frustrating." The manager Tracy reports the improvements subtle and the goal unchanged: to have him for the Wild Card opener Tuesday, most likely in the Bronx. And the ward notes with a wry pen that Houston's misfortune was Houston's making: it was Daulton Varsho's ailing wrist that summoned Lucas Spence from the taxi squad on Wednesday — and the whole of the front page above is what the replacement did with the summons.

THE REMEMBRANCE DESK: TEN YEARS SINCE JOSÉ DAY WENT DARK — THE GAME MARKS A DECADE WITHOUT FERNÁNDEZ

Ten years ago this very morning — the five-and-twentieth of September, 2016 — the game woke to the news that José Fernández was dead at four-and-twenty, lost with two others when his boat went down off Miami in the night. A decade on, the wound keeps its edge. Before Misiorowski and Skenes were appointment viewing, there was José Day, every fifth afternoon in Little Havana, when the ballpark of the Marlins became the place to be in all South Florida — a Cuban boy who fled the island by boat with his mother, and grew into the American Dream in flannels, throwing fire with a grin that filled the building. "He was a ball of energy," remembers Ramos, his old bullpen mate, now at the broadcast table. "That was his superpower — you just felt it when he was around." His teammates of that morning still tell of the clubhouse with the blank stares, the game called without a reason given, the reason understood soon enough.

The Herald kept its colors lowered a long while that autumn, and lowers them again a moment now. Some careers are measured in what was done; his is measured also in what was plainly coming, and the game is ten years poorer for never seeing it. The paper marks the decade, and keeps the name.

THE ALMANAC DESK: A STORM RIDES FOR NEW ENGLAND AND THE SCHEDULE BENDS BEFORE IT — TWIN BILLS BOOKEND THIS DAY, SATURDAY BELONGS TO VERLANDER, AND THE SCHERZER WIRE STAYS SILENT

The weather has taken a hand in the wild-card arithmetic. With a great storm forecast to strike New England this very weekend, the Cubs' Sunday engagement at Fenway Park has been moved forward, so that today's card carries a separate-admission twin bill at Boston — the first game at 1:05, the second at 6:05 — with Saturday evening's contest still scheduled and, by the manager Counsell's cheerful accounting, everything thereafter at the storm's pleasure. "Whatever you want to make us do, we'll do it," said he, a man lately relieved of his clinching worries. "Let's go." The Bronx carries a twin bill of its own this afternoon, Baltimore visiting the Yankees twice before the weekend's page turns.

Two appointments stand ahead. Saturday at 1:10 at Comerica Park, Justin Verlander takes a big-league mound for the last time, against the visiting Pirates — the farewell this paper has kept watch upon all week, and no ceremonial inning if the man himself has any say. And of Max Scherzer, who told the press Wednesday that word on his future would likely come within a day or two, the wires this morning carry nothing yet — the Herald checked both desks and will keep checking. The season's last page falls Sunday the seven-and-twentieth; the Wild Card rounds open Tuesday the nine-and-twentieth.

The Rest of the Card

THE CENTURY IS BANKED AND THE FIRST SEED WITH IT — CHOURIO WALKS, RUNS, AND RETURNS TO STRIKE THE HUNDREDTH'S EXCLAMATION POINT: CREAM CITY NINE 5, QUAKERS 1

The hundredth win this paper saw waiting on Thursday's card arrived on schedule, and with flourishes: tied at one in the eighth, Jackson Chourio pinch-hit for Contreras — lifted for want of hustle on a groundout — walked, stole second, and scored on Bauers' single, whereupon Pratt and Ortiz singled home two more and Chourio returned in the ninth to hit his five-and-twentieth home run for good measure. So Milwaukee stands at a hundred victories, the first club to reach the figure since 2023, the first of the Central since the 2016 Cubs, and the first in the franchise's whole history — the Brewers leaving behind the company of the seven clubs that had never — all without ever winning more than five games running, a thing no hundred-win club had managed before. By midnight, Los Angeles having lost, the National's first seed and home ground throughout were Milwaukee's outright. "I've never been on a 100-win team before," said Bauers, whose go-ahead knock followed what he called a mental recalibration in the batting cage. "Not many people have." Philadelphia's evening, and Arraez's ankle, are entered at the ward; the Quakers' clinch must now wait upon the weekend.

ONE SWING AROUND THE PESKY POLE IS THE WHOLE OF THE SCORING — CANTILLO AND SMITH SEAL CLEVELAND'S THIRD OCTOBER RUNNING: CLEVELAND NINE 1, CRIMSON HOSE 0

Angel Martínez supplied the game's lone run in the second — a 319-foot chip shot by the measuring instruments, curled just around the Pesky Pole in Fenway's right corner, his eighteenth — and Cleveland's arms made it stand: Cantillo took the decision to eleven victories, and Cade Smith closed his one-and-fortieth save, the American's leading figure, against a Boston order held to two hits entire. The victory clinches the Cleveland nine's third consecutive October and the nineteenth berth in the franchise book, with the larger prize still live: the Central's lead stands at one over Chicago with three to play, the tiebreaker Chicago's, the closing hands dealt at the October desk. "One pitch at a time, one day at a time," said Martínez amid the champagne. "Right now, it's time to enjoy. Tomorrow is another day." Boston's greater worry wore a splint, as the ward relates.

FIVE YEARS OF WANDERING END IN AN AFTERNOON — SIX RUNS INSIDE TWO INNINGS AND THE WHITE STOCKINGS TAKE THEIR OCTOBER CHAIR: WHITE STOCKINGS 9, MISSOURIANS 1

The clinch that slipped Chicago's grasp on Wednesday was seized without ceremony on Thursday: six runs inside the first two innings at Kansas City — Vargas singling home a pair, Teel crossing three times and adding his fifth home run in the fourth — and the Missourians' answer confined to Perez's twentieth. Sandlin took the decision, and the South Side is seated in October for the first time since it won the Central of 2021, three seasons of a hundred defeats now formally behind it. "Everybody in here is really friends with each other. There's no egos at all," said Benintendi, who has seen the lean years from inside. "It's been a lot more enjoyable this year." The larger prize stays live: one game behind Cleveland with three to play, the season-series tiebreaker in hand, and Colorado arriving on the South Side tonight.

BOYD'S GEM AND HAPP'S THREE-BAGGER UNCORK WRIGLEY AT LAST — THE NORTH SIDERS CLINCH ON THEIR FINAL HOME HAND: NORTH SIDERS 2, FLORIDIANS 1

Twice the champagne had waited on ice, and on the season's last Wrigley afternoon it waited no longer. Matthew Boyd, the Opening Day man, gave the must-win game a gem for his tenth victory; Marsee's third-inning single had Miami ahead until Suzuki's six-and-twentieth squared it in the fifth; and in the sixth the longest-tenured Cub, Ian Happ, legged a triple and came home on Hoerner's single, Zeferjahn sealing the seventh save. The berth is Chicago's — a second consecutive October for the first time since the run of 2015 through '18 — and Crow-Armstrong's first-inning theft, which put him in a registry of six other names, is sung at the milestone desk. "To be able to celebrate together after all we've been through is pretty cool," said Swanson from behind ski goggles. The road closes the account: three at Fenway, weather permitting, as the almanac explains.

A THREE-RUN SEVENTH SETTLES THE CHAMPIONS AND A FRANCHISE FIRST IS BANKED — THE SAN DIEGO NINE CLINCH, AND HAND MILWAUKEE THE SEED BESIDES: SAN DIEGO NINE 4, ANGELENOS 2

Scoreless into the sixth, the San Diego nine pried the evening open by inches — Harris' sacrifice fly, then a three-run seventh stitched from singles by Hays, the young catcher Salas, and Tatis, who stole two bases besides — while Matsui took the decision over Glasnow and Mason Miller sealed his eight-and-thirtieth save against Ohtani's ninth-inning double. The victory clinches a berth: a third consecutive autumn of October baseball for the first time in the franchise's history, and a fifth in seven years, for a club that sat three games under the even mark in late July amid an eight-game losing streak. "It was do or die," Cronenworth said of those weeks; the deliverance was the bullpen scheme the clubhouse came to call pitching chaos. The defeat cost Los Angeles any claim on the National's first seed, which passed to Milwaukee by the tiebreaker's terms — and these same two clubs play out the string while Arizona arrives in San Diego with designs of its own, as the October desk relates.

FOUR RUNS DOWN, THE PINSTRIPES SEND A FOOTBALLER'S FEET AROUND THE BASES — LOMBARD'S SLIDE, THEN LOMBARD'S THUNDER, TURN THE EVENING ENTIRE: PINSTRIPES 6, SUNSHINE NINE 4

The crowned Rays led four-to-nothing by the sixth — Caminero twice singling home Díaz toward his nine-and-ninetieth run driven in — whereupon the Bronx staged its recovery around a rookie's ankles. Wells' fourteenth home run opened the account; in the seventh George Lombard Jr. doubled home a run and then, with Hopkins' hundred-mile fastball at the backstop, came flying down the line to stop short of the catcher's tag and slap the plate with his hand — a piece of footwork his soccer boyhood explains and the moving pictures have already immortalized — Goldschmidt's knock squaring the game behind him. In the eighth Lombard settled matters with a two-run blow to the second deck, his seventh: at one-and-twenty years and 114 days, the second-youngest Yankee ever to hit a go-ahead homer so late in a game, behind only the Mantle of 1952. "I was in trouble, had to figure something out, and it just kind of happened," said the rookie of the slide. His manager Boone, of the homer: "Absolutely scalded... It's really good to see that."

SIX IN THE FIRST AND EIGHTEEN HITS ENTIRE — THE DESERT NINE COMPLETE THE SWEEP AND CARRY FIVE STRAIGHT INTO SAN DIEGO: DESERT NINE 12, MOUNTAIN MEN 8

Arizona fell upon Denver for six in the first inning — Moreno's three-run homer and Arenado's nine-and-twentieth the heavy blows — and piled eighteen hits in all, McCann homering and driving in two while Eduardo Rodriguez took his sixteenth victory, second-most in the National. Colorado's late thunder — Carrigg's three-run blow among five home runs of the home nine's own — made the score honest without ever making it close. The sweep is Arizona's fifth consecutive victory and keeps the executioner waiting yet again: two games behind Philadelphia with three to play, the path running through San Diego and requiring at least two victories there beside a Tampa Bay service at Philadelphia. "The focus and the talk in the clubhouse has been go 1-0 every day," said McCann. "That's what we've done so far."

ROCKER'S FINEST HOUR AND TWO THUNDERCLAPS KEEP THE THRONE SHARED — THE TEXAS NINE REFUSE TO BLINK FIRST: TEXAS NINE 3, AMAZINS 1

A night after watching Seattle rescue them on the clubhouse televisions, the Rangers rescued themselves: Kumar Rocker turned in one of the finest appearances of his season, Jung's two-run homer answered New York's first-inning run before the frame was out, Seager added his nineteenth in the sixth, and Montgomery sealed his first save. The victory put Texas alone atop the West for some hours, until Houston's evening — the account at the head of this paper — restored the dead heat by midnight. "There's still a pulse. As long as we still have a pulse, we're good to go," said the manager Schumaker, whose club opens its final three at Minnesota tonight. "The scoreboard watching is more fun when you win."

SKENES BANKS TWO HUNDRED AND THE BULLPEN BANKS THE VERDICT — HORWITZ'S EIGHTH-INNING FLY OUTWEIGHS BURLESON'S LEADOFF THUNDER: BUCS 2, REDBIRDS 1

Alec Burleson opened the game with his four-and-twentieth home run — the hundred-and-thirteenth run he has driven home this year, the National's leading figure — and St. Louis got nothing further; Lowe singled home Cruz to square it in the first, and Horwitz's sacrifice fly cashed Simon in the eighth. Skenes struck out his two-hundredth of the season along the way, as the milestone desk sings, with Weaver taking the decision in relief and Montgomery sealing his seventeenth save. The Bucs thus reach one-and-eighty victories playing loose and dangerous; the Redbirds, whose catcher Herrera was charged with two of the evening's errors, play out the string at Milwaukee from tonight.

JORGE'S FIRST AND DE LA CRUZ'S THIRTIETH OUTVOTE THE CHAMPIONS — RODRÍGUEZ'S SIXTH SETTLES A SEESAW AT TRUIST: REDLEGS 7, ATLANTAS 6

On the night a Houston rookie hit his first three home runs, the Redlegs' Carlos Jorge led off the whole evening with the first of his own career — and Atlanta answered with four in the home first, whereupon the two nines traded the lead like men passing a hot stone. Elly De La Cruz reached thirty home runs in the third, Suárez's two-run single gave Cincinnati five, Riley's nineteenth squared the account at five, and Héctor Rodríguez's two-run blow in the sixth — his sixth — proved the last word, Pagán sealing his five-and-twentieth save. The crowned champions of the East, at three-and-ninety wins, lost nothing they need but the evening; the spoilers of the Queen City have now beaten them twice running.

MOORE'S BAT DOES THE HEAVY CARRYING AND THE SERAPHS PLAY SPOILER BY THE SOUND — WOO'S TWELVE VICTORIES CANNOT SURVIVE THE SIXTH: SERAPHS 6, SEATTLE NINE 4

The young second baseman Christian Moore drove home three — a single in the second, the tying pressure of the fifth, and a two-run double off Woo in the sixth that turned the game for good — while Teodosio added two runs driven in of his own and Watson sealed the fourth save. Julio Rodríguez's two-and-twentieth home run had built Seattle's early lead, and it did not hold. The Seattle nine, one night removed from deranging the West's arithmetic in ten innings, thus surrender the favor to the last-place Seraphs; the Angels, at one-and-sixty wins, seem determined to spend the season's final days inconveniencing their betters.

The Friday tables, then — twelve contests entered, four clinches recorded, and three questions left standing with three days to answer them. In the American: Tampa Bay holds the first seed at six-and-ninety wins; New York hosts the Wild Card round from Tuesday the nine-and-twentieth; the Central is Cleveland's by one over Chicago with the tiebreaker in the White Sox' keeping — Cleveland closes three at Kansas City, Chicago hosts Colorado — and the West remains a dead heat at nine-and-seventy wins, Houston closing three at the Athletics with the Silver Boot tiebreaker in hand while Texas plays three at Minnesota; the division's loser goes home. In the National: Milwaukee, at a hundred wins, holds the first seed and home ground throughout; Los Angeles and Atlanta are crowned; San Diego and the Cubs are seated in the wild-card row with the order still to be settled; and the last chair is Philadelphia's by two over Arizona, the Quakers hosting Tampa Bay while the Desert nine visit San Diego needing two victories of three and a service from the Sunshine nine besides. Today's bill of seventeen, verified against the schedule: twin bills at Fenway Park — 1:05 and 6:05, the storm's doing — and in the Bronx, Baltimore visiting twice from 4 o'clock; Pittsburgh at Detroit and Tampa Bay at Philadelphia at 6:40, Sánchez and his eighteen victories taking the ball for the Quakers; the Mets at Washington at 6:45; Cincinnati at Toronto at 7:07; Atlanta at Miami at 7:10; St. Louis at Milwaukee, Cleveland at Kansas City — Williams and his fourteen wins on the hill — and Colorado at the White Sox, all at 7:40; Texas at Minnesota at 8:10, deGrom taking the ball; Arizona at San Diego and Houston at the Athletics at 9:40; the Angels at Seattle at 10:10; and the champions at San Francisco at 10:15. Tomorrow belongs to Verlander at Comerica, and Sunday the seven-and-twentieth is the season's last page, with the Wild Card rounds from Tuesday. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: FOUR-AND-FORTY PITCHES BUY HOUSTON NO PEACE — HADER WALKS THE BASES FULL IN THE TENTH, NAYLOR EMPTIES THEM, AND THE WEST'S DEAD HEAT SURVIVES THE NIGHT: MARINERS 6, ASTROS 5, IN TEN INNINGS
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 78 · Thursday, the Four-and-Twentieth of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 16 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

FOUR-AND-FORTY PITCHES BUY HOUSTON NO PEACE — HADER WALKS THE BASES FULL IN THE TENTH, NAYLOR EMPTIES THEM, AND THE WEST'S DEAD HEAT SURVIVES THE NIGHT: MARINERS 6, ASTROS 5, IN TEN INNINGS

Houston builds a four-run lead by the third and watches Seattle claw it level; Diaz's tenth-inning triple restores the advantage and the rested Hader is sent back out to keep it; whereupon three walks in four batsmen — Rodríguez forcing home the tie with the bases loaded — and Naylor's line single undo the whole evening's work; Texas beaten at home besides, the throne stays shared at eight-and-seventy wins apiece with four to play, the tiebreaker still in Houston's keeping

Josh Hader had already spent nineteen pitches on the ninth inning when the manager Espada sent him back out for the tenth, and no one in the American's maddest division would call the decision timid: Texas had already lost at Arlington, and one Houston victory would have seized sole command of a West that has refused all season to be commanded. "We used our entire arsenal there trying to get through that one," Espada said afterward, which was the plain truth — and the arsenal was not enough.

For three innings the evening had gone entirely to Houston's design. Altuve's single — a ball that struck an umpire on its way through the infield — cashed the first run, Paredes lifted a sacrifice fly, and Yainer Diaz drove his fourteenth home run to left with Alvarez aboard: four to nothing before Seattle had drawn a breath. The mariners of the Sound answered in the home third with Canzone's two-run knock and Rodríguez's run-scoring double, squared the account at four on Canzone's single in the fifth, and then the two nines played six scoreless innings of the tautest September baseball while the scoreboard watchers in two time zones kept their sums. In the tenth Diaz struck again — a triple, his first three-bagger of the season, sent to the right-field line to fetch home Alvarez — and Houston stood three outs from the division's sole lead.

Whereupon the tenth's bottom half arrived, and Hader — five days rested, his sinker running to 96 — could not find the plate. Three of the four men he faced walked, Julio Rodríguez taking the last of them with the bases loaded to force the tie, and Josh Naylor lined the next offering to center to end it. Four-and-forty pitches the closer threw in all, tied for the fifth-heaviest night of his career and his heaviest since 2019. "It sucks that we lost this one and how we did," Hader owned, "but we've still got the tiebreaker and that's fortunate for us — we can't bank on that. We've got to win out." So the dead heat this paper entered Wednesday survives its first test intact: Houston and Texas level at eight-and-seventy wins, four to play — the Astros' four all at the ninety-five-times-beaten Athletics, the Rangers closing with the Mets this afternoon before three at Minnesota — and the Silver Boot tiebreaker still says the West is Houston's to win if Houston simply refuses to lose. Wednesday it did not refuse; it merely ran out of strikes.

News Around the League

THE OCTOBER DESK: THE WEST'S DEAD HEAT HOLDS, TORONTO'S CANDLE GOES OUT AT LAST — AND THE PALE HOSE AND THE FRIARS EACH STAND ONE RESULT FROM A BERTH

The American's West survived the wildest night of its dead heat unchanged — Houston beaten in ten at Seattle as the account above relates, Texas beaten at home by the eliminated Mets — so both clubs stand at eight-and-seventy wins with four to play and Houston's tiebreaker still governing. And the same day closed one ledger for good: Toronto, champion of the American League a year ago, was formally eliminated when the first game of the Baltimore twin bill went against it, the fall from pennant to autumn silence complete in a single calendar's turn.

The two nearest berths may be clinched this very day. The White Sox, beaten five-to-four at Kansas City on Garcia's seventh-inning double, need one victory or one Texas defeat to seat themselves in October for the first time since 2021 — the front office traveled to Kansas City Wednesday for what might have been the festivities, and got a lesson in presumption for its trouble. Their larger prize stays live besides: Cleveland's shutout defeat at Boston keeps the Central's gap at one game, and Chicago holds the season-series tiebreaker, seven games to six. In the National, San Diego's victory at Los Angeles put the Friars one step from the postseason — one win, or one Arizona defeat at Denver this afternoon, clinches — while the Cubs and Phillies both lost and sit knotted at seven-and-eighty wins for the second wild-card chair, Chicago holding the tiebreaker over Philadelphia and San Diego alike. Arizona, alive by its own hand, stands three back of the third chair with four to play.

One almanac note with October consequence: foul weather forecast for Boston has moved the Cubs' Saturday engagement forward, so Chicago now plays a separate-admission twin bill at Fenway Park on Friday — a scheduling hand the manager Counsell reckons was dealt against him, with his club still chasing its clinch. "It always kind of seems like the baseball gods are going to test you," said his pitcher Gausman, "and it always seems to come at a time when you don't want it to."

THE MILESTONE DESK: FOUR MEN NOW SHARE THE AMERICAN'S HOME-RUN CROWN AT ONE-AND-FORTY — AND SALE BANKS A NINTH SEASON OF TWO HUNDRED STRIKEOUTS

The American's home-run race, which began the week as one man's story, ended Wednesday as a four-part harmony. Pete Alonso — whose fortieth this paper sang on Tuesday to the strains of Earth, Wind & Fire — struck his one-and-fortieth in the twin bill's opener at Camden Yards, and by nightfall Ben Rice of the Yankees had hit two in a single game, his fortieth and one-and-fortieth, to draw level with Alonso, with Houston's Alvarez, and with Tampa Bay's Caminero. Four men, one number, four days remaining. Rice's pair carried its own footnote: the manager Boone had prophesied him thirty-nine home runs in the spring, and Rice took the figure as an insult to be avenged. "I was pretty close, but he went soaring past," Boone allowed. The young man is the thirteenth Yankee ever to reach forty, and only Judge and DiMaggio managed it within their first three seasons in that uniform. In the National the arithmetic holds one rung higher: Crow-Armstrong and Schwarber share the lead at five-and-forty, with Atlanta's Olson joining the one-and-forty club Wednesday by a blow of his own.

At Truist Park, Chris Sale struck out ten Cincinnati batsmen in his final tuning before October and, with the last of them, banked his two-hundredth strikeout of the year — the ninth season of two hundred in his career, a company few living arms keep. He had ended the fifth inning at 199 and asked to go back out. "I told myself before this game that I really wanted to make it feel like a playoff game," said the southpaw, who takes the ball for the first game of the Wild Card round Tuesday. The evening asked more of him than strikeouts, as the colors desk below records.

THE FAREWELL DESK: APPEARANCE FIVE HUNDRED, AND AN ANNOUNCEMENT WITHIN DAYS — SCHERZER POINTS THE FINGER AT HIMSELF AND ASKS FOR THE BALL ONE MORE SUNDAY

Max Scherzer took the mound at Baltimore Wednesday for the five-hundredth appearance of his career — the four-hundred-ninety-first of them a start — and left it beaten, four runs in five innings, undone chiefly by Alonso's milestone blow. Afterward the two-and-forty-year-old said plainly that he will likely have something to say about his future within a day or two, and that he hopes to return on short rest for Sunday's season finale. The self-accounting he offered meanwhile was the old competitor's, unsoftened: "Instead of pointing the finger at everybody else, I'll point the finger at myself and what I've done this year. I got beat on one pitch here. I feel like I've said that a lot, but that's the big leagues."

The week thus carries two farewells in close formation: Verlander's final start comes Saturday at Detroit, as this paper recorded Wednesday, and Scherzer's reckoning — whatever he announces — follows hard upon. Two of the age's great right arms, whose duels ornamented a decade of Octobers, reaching the same page of the calendar together; the Herald will keep both accounts with care.

THE HERALD LOWERS ITS COLORS: DON COOPER, WHO TAUGHT THE SOUTH SIDE ITS PITCHING FOR THREE-AND-THIRTY YEARS, IS DEAD AT SEVENTY

Word came Wednesday, confirmed by his family, that Don Cooper — Coop to every man who ever threw a baseball in his sight — has died at seventy. He served the White Sox organization three-and-thirty seasons from 1988 through 2020, eighteen of them as the big club's pitching coach, and his monument is the 2005 championship staff that threw four consecutive complete games in the League Championship Series before sweeping the World Series — a feat of preparation as much as of arms. The testimony poured in from his fraternity: Contreras, who said losing him felt like losing family; Konerko, who remembered a man who "could talk somebody up into thinking they were good"; and Sale, who learned the news moments before his warmups Wednesday and went out and struck out ten. "I wouldn't be here without him," said the southpaw, whose first big-league pitching coach Cooper was.

That his passing came on a night his old organization stood a single result from its first October in five years is the kind of arithmetic Coop would have waved off with something fast-talking and unprintable. The Herald lowers its colors for a teacher of the craft: the game is subtracted by his going, and every pitcher he ever talked into believing himself good is the proof of what it gained by his staying so long.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: JUDGE VOWS THE BRONX WILL NOT OPEN OCTOBER WITHOUT HIM — RAFAELA'S RETURN LASTS SEVEN OUTS, AND GAUSMAN'S SHOULDER JOINS THE WATCH

Aaron Judge spoke Wednesday like a man arguing with a calendar. The captain, shelved Saturday with what his manager called a moderate strain of the right calf — the soleus, Judge specified, a muscle "a little more crucial with running and hitting" — received a plasma injection Monday and intends to be ready for the first game of the Wild Card round Tuesday in the Bronx. "The Bronx is a magical place in October," he said. "I don't want to miss out on that opportunity." Boone, after the nine-run evening entered on the card below, would rule nothing out: "We're going to listen to the body and see how he heals. If he's in a position to play, obviously we're going to want him."

At Boston the ward giveth and taketh in the same evening: Ceddanne Rafaela, back from three weeks on the shelf, opened the game with a diving, extra-base-robbing catch and lined a single in the second — then came up lame down the line, right hamstring tight, and was gone before the third. The pictures are ordered; the man himself professed little alarm. At Wrigley Field, Kevin Gausman left a fine outing with trouble in the left shoulder that his club prays does not linger, a subtraction the wild-card arithmetic can ill afford. And at Kansas City, Erick Fedde took a 104-mile-an-hour drive off the right calf in the second inning, pitched on, and limped to his locker afterward with clean X-rays — the White Sox will call it a bruise and a bargain.

THE CONVALESCENT DESK: THE VIGIL CLOSES WITH A LINE SINGLE TO RIGHT — OHTANI RETURNS TO THE CHAMPIONS' ORDER, AND CHAPMAN COMES BACK THROWING LIGHTNING

The watch this paper has kept over Shohei Ohtani — the named day, the manager's promise, the batting-order deliberations — closed Wednesday night at Chavez Ravine precisely as promised. Activated from his fifteen-day shelf-leave, batting second for the first time all year, he lined the evening's first plate appearance into right field for a single, walked in the third, and finished one-for-four in a defeat the card below records. The verdict wanted was health, not heroics, and health is what the eye reported: "There wasn't any chase," said the manager Roberts. "When you feel healthy and strong, you feel like you can just see the baseball, trust your eyes and take your swing. I thought that's what you saw tonight." The operations chief Friedman wants only at-bats now — "as many as we can, some rhythm and timing" — with five games to sharpen the sword before October.

At Fenway the convalescence ran ahead of schedule: Aroldis Chapman, silent since the thirteenth with a balky lat, returned to strike out the side — all three swinging, twelve pitches — for the four-hundred-second save of his career and five-and-thirtieth of the year. "I feel normal. I feel like I'm at a hundred percent right now," said the eight-and-thirty-year-old, and the Guardians who faced him offered no rebuttal.

THE CURIOSITIES DESK: A TWIN BILL UMPIRED BY TWINS — THE BROTHERS JONES MAKE HISTORY AT CAMDEN YARDS, AND A PITCHER IN AMARILLO CELEBRATES A PENNANT UPSIDE DOWN

The doubleheader at Baltimore carried a wonder in plain sight: Austin and Tyler Jones, identical twins of Charleston, became the first such pair ever to serve on the same umpiring crew in a Major League game — Austin at first base and Tyler at second for the opener, the two swapping stations for the nightcap. Umpires together since the age of fifteen, schooled together at eighteen, they had crossed paths professionally almost never in a dozen years of minor-league roads. "This is something we've dreamed about forever," said Tyler. That the twin bill they worked produced twin scores — Baltimore four, Toronto two, twice over, as the card below attests — is the sort of coincidence this paper declines to explain and simply enters in the book.

And in the Texas League, the Diamondbacks' young right-hander Alfred Morillo closed Double-A Amarillo's championship victory Wednesday with a 97-mile-an-hour strikeout — and then, as he did upon clinching the finals berth last week, turned a full standing backflip on the mound and stuck the landing. The parent club's manager Lovullo, shown the earlier rendition, reviewed it as an aesthete and a worrier at once: "That's pretty impressive. Yeah, that's hard to do."

The Rest of the Card

FOUR THUNDERCLAPS AND A GRAND SLAM FROM McMAHON — RICE SOARS PAST HIS MANAGER'S PROPHECY TO A SHARE OF THE CROWN: BOMBERS 9, GULF COAST CLUB 2

The Bombers made short work of the newly crowned division champions: Rice's fortieth home run in the first, McMahon's grand slam in a five-run third, the youngster Lombard Jr.'s sixth, and Rice again in the fourth for the one-and-fortieth that ties the American's home-run lead four ways, as the milestone desk relates. Cole took the decision to ten victories, and Tampa Bay's answer — DeLuca's three hits and two thefts, Mullins' answering blow — never threatened the account. Tonight the same two nines send Seymour against Schlittler and his league-best 1.94 earned-run figure.

ALONSO'S ONE-AND-FORTIETH SETTLES THE MATINEE AND TORONTO'S CANDLE GOES OUT — SCHERZER'S FIVE-HUNDREDTH APPEARANCE ENDS IN DEFEAT: BIRDS 4, MAPLE LEAF NINE 2

The opener of the Camden Yards twin bill turned on one swing: with Baltimore ahead two, Pete Alonso met a Scherzer offering in the fifth and sent it to left center with Beavers aboard — the one-and-fortieth, and the blow that formally snuffed Toronto's October candle, guttering since this paper first marked it Monday. Bassitt took the decision to nine wins, Kittredge sealed the save, and the two runs Toronto scratched back in the sixth, gifted on a throwing error, fell short by the very margin of Alonso's stroke. Scherzer's own reckoning, and the farewell it may portend, stands at the desk above; the elimination closes Toronto's ledger one year after a pennant.

THE NIGHTCAP COPIES THE MATINEE TO THE VERY DIGIT — TREY GIBSON THROWS SIX AND TWO-THIRDS SPOTLESS AND THE SWEEP IS TWINS ALL THE WAY DOWN: BALTIMORES 4, BLUE JAYS 2

The second game ended precisely as the first — four to two, Baltimore — and the symmetry extended to the men in blue, as the curiosities desk records. Trey Gibson supplied the substance: six and two-thirds scoreless innings with seven strikeouts, while Encarnacion-Strand drove home three — a two-run single in the first and his eleventh home run in the fourth — and Cowser doubled home the other. Toronto's whole evening was Schneider's two-run blow in the ninth. The Birds ride three straight victories and, at eight-and-seventy wins, keep a mathematician's breath of wild-card life at three games and a half from Chicago's chair with three to play.

TWELVE HITS BUY ONE RUN, AND ONE RUN IS RICHES — GRAY'S EIGHTEENTH AND CHAPMAN'S FOUR-HUNDRED-SECOND CLOSE THE WHITEWASH: FENWAY MEN 1, LAKE ERIE MEN 0

Sonny Gray closed his regular season with six scoreless innings on a mere seven-and-seventy pitches — the league lead in victories now his at eighteen against five — and Chapman, back from the shelf, struck out the side in the ninth for the save, as the convalescent desk sings. Boston stacked twelve hits and cashed exactly one, Monasterio's sixth-inning single fetching Duran home, and one sufficed; Griffin, beaten despite a fine account, falls to fifteen-and-six. Cleveland's six-game winning streak dies at Fenway, though the Central's lead survives the night at one, Chicago having stumbled in its turn.

THE PARTY WAITS IN THE LUGGAGE — GARCIA'S SEVENTH-INNING DOUBLE HOLDS OFF THE PALE HOSE BY ONE: KANSAS CITY NINE 5, PALE HOSE 4

Kansas City struck four in the first off the opener Hudson, Chicago clawed all four back in the third — Teel's two-run single and Murakami's double the heart of it — and there the matter stood until Maikel Garcia doubled home Witt with two out in the seventh. Antonacci's deep fly died at the center-field track to end it. The defeat postpones a clinch the White Sox front office had traveled to witness: one victory, or one Texas defeat, seats the South Side in October for the first time since 2021, and the Central remains but a single game distant with the tiebreaker in Chicago's keeping — the arithmetic is at the October desk, and Fedde's bruised calf at the ward.

SALE STRIKES OUT TEN WITH A HEAVY HEART AND DUBÓN SETTLES IT IN THE TENTH: TOMAHAWK NINE 3, QUEEN CITY NINE 2

An evening that began with hard news — Sale learning of his old teacher Cooper's death moments before his warmups, as the colors desk mourns — ended in a walk-off: Mauricio Dubón singled home Keirsey Jr. in the tenth to give the crowned champions of the East their victory. Between the two, Sale struck out ten across five and two-thirds for his two-hundredth of the year, Olson squared the game with his one-and-fortieth home run, and Riley's eighteenth answered Cincinnati's seventh-inning lead. Abbott's seven strong innings for the Queen City nine deserved better company; Suter took the decision.

TURANG AND YELICH STRIKE IN THE OPENING FRAMES AND VICTORY NINE-AND-NINETY IS BANKED — THE HUNDREDTH WAITS ON TONIGHT: SUDS MEN 4, PHILADELPHIAS 1

Turang led off the game with his twentieth home run, Yelich added his twelfth an inning later, and Contreras' two-run single in the third completed all the scoring Milwaukee required; Henderson took the decision to eleven wins against three, and Megill sealed his thirtieth save. Nola struck out eight in defeat, Realmuto's groundout cashing Philadelphia's lone run. The Suds men stand at nine-and-ninety victories — one more, and they enter the game's hundred-win registry for the first time since the 2016 Cubs took the Central — with the chance at it this evening in the same park.

FIVE UNANSWERED AFTER LOWE'S EARLY THUNDER — THE MOUND CITY NINE END PITTSBURGH'S STREAK AT FIVE: MOUND CITY NINE 5, BUCCANEERS 1

Lowe's four-and-thirtieth home run gave Pittsburgh the second inning, and nothing thereafter belonged to the home nine: Burleson's single squared it — his league-leading hundred-and-twelfth run driven in — Bernal singled home two more, and Winn and Wetherholt stitched the fourth and fifth runs nose to tail. Liberatore took the decision, and Eisert the loss. The Buccaneers' five-game run, which had made September ask permission of no one, closes at eighty wins; St. Louis plays out its string with the spoiler's relish, and the same two nines meet again at midday.

PERFECT THROUGH FOUR AND SPOILERS TO THE LAST — McLEAN'S SEVEN INNINGS AND BATY'S NINTH-INNING SLAM SINK ARLINGTON DEEPER: FLUSHING NINE 7, ARLINGTON MEN 2

Nolan McLean retired the first twelve Texas batsmen in order and finished seven innings of two runs for his twelfth victory, while Soto's seven-and-twentieth home run built the early lead; when Texas squared it at two in the fifth, Semien answered with a blow in the eighth and Brett Baty broke the thing open with a grand slam in the ninth. The eliminated Flushing nine thus play executioner in a race not their own: the defeat is Arlington's third straight and drops the first home series since July, the West's arithmetic — must-win now, by the first baseman Burger's own accounting — entered at the October desk.

FOUR UNEARNED IN THE FIRST KEEP THE EXECUTIONER WAITING — THE SONORAN NINE LIVE TO FIGHT ANOTHER DAY: SONORAN NINE 5, COLORADANS 3

An error in left by Veen opened the gate in the first, and Arizona marched four unearned runs through it — Moreno and Arenado singling runs home, Carroll tripling home two more — before Tawa's eleventh home run supplied the fifth in the eighth. Kelly took the decision and Loáisiga the save against Colorado's scattered answers. The victory means the Sonoran nine cannot yet be eliminated, and the day's losses in Chicago and Philadelphia pulled them to three games from the last wild-card chair with four to play; this afternoon's finale at Denver doubles as San Diego's clinch-watch, as the October desk explains.

THE FISH KEEP WRIGLEY'S CHAMPAGNE ON ICE YET ANOTHER NIGHT — AN OVERTURNED CALL AT SECOND CASHES THE WINNER: FISH 3, CUBS 2

Stowers' one-and-twentieth home run — the lone blemish on Gausman's evening before the shoulder trouble entered at the ward — had Miami ahead until Swanson's two-run single squared it in the sixth; whereupon the seventh turned on the moving pictures, a challenged force play at second overturned to let Ramírez score the go-ahead run on Mack's grounder. Alcantara sealed it. The Cubs are two-for-six-and-twenty with runners in scoring position across the two defeats, the win-and-in box now unchecked a second consecutive night, and the wild-card knot at the October desk grows no gentler for the waiting.

WALTON'S THREE-RUN BLOW SETTLES MATTERS EARLY AND THE WHITE ELEPHANTS TRAMPLE ON — TROUT'S TWO-AND-TWENTIETH IS ANSWER ENOUGH FOR NOBODY: WHITE ELEPHANTS 7, ANAHEIM NINE 3

Five runs inside two innings — Butler's run-scoring knock, Walton's three-run homer, Bolte's double — decided the West Sacramento evening before it fairly began, and Langeliers' two-run double in the sixth answered Anaheim's middle-innings push. Trout's two-and-twentieth home run and Grissom's thirteenth made it briefly respectable; Hartlieb took the decision, and Ureña the defeat. The Athletics, at three-and-sixty wins, now host Houston for four with the West's throne in the balance — the spoiler's chair is theirs if they care to sit in it.

A SCORELESS KNOT CUT IN THE SIXTH BY ABRAMS AND MORALES — THE WASHINGTONS TAKE THE SERIES FROM THE MOTOR CITY NINE: WASHINGTONS 4, TIGERS 2

Five and a half innings of nothing gave way all at once: Abrams lined home the first run and Yohandy Morales followed with a two-run homer, his fourth, before Wood's groundout cashed a fourth run in the seventh. Malgeri — the No. 53 whose deeds christened the newly renamed park in Monday's account — answered with a home run and a late run-scoring single, but Dion and the Washington relief corps held, Cruz sealing the save. Detroit, at four-and-seventy wins, turns its eyes wholly to Saturday and Verlander's farewell; the visiting Pirates arrive Friday.

KEASCHALL'S BAT BOOKENDS THE AFTERNOON AND GÓMEZ HOLDS THE MIDDLE — THE NORTH STARS TAKE THE RUBBER MATCH BY THE BAY: NORTH STARS 4, JINTS 2

The young Keaschall opened the scoring with his tenth home run in the third and squared the game with a sacrifice fly in the fifth after Whitcomb's two-run single had given San Francisco the lead; Jenkins and Bell singled home the deciding runs in the seventh, nose to tail. Gómez took the decision and Morris his fifth save. Minnesota thus claims the series two games to one and heads home to receive Texas for the season's final three — an engagement the West's dead heat has made consequential far beyond the Twin Cities' own concluded ambitions.

MACHADO GREETS THE GREAT RETURN WITH THUNDER OF HIS OWN — THE FRIARS STAND ONE STEP FROM OCTOBER: FRIARS 5, DODGERS 1

On the night Ohtani rejoined the champions' order, as the convalescent desk relates, the visitors wrote the larger headline: Manny Machado's nine-and-twentieth home run put San Diego ahead in the fourth, his sacrifice fly and a Yamamoto throwing error built the fifth inning's two, and Fermin singled home a fifth in the ninth. Rodriguez took the decision over Yamamoto, whose fourteen victories could not survive the evening's bookkeeping. The Friars, at eight-and-eighty wins, hold the wild-card row's head chair by one and may clinch a berth before tonight's first pitch — by Arizona's defeat this afternoon, or failing that by their own hand against these same Dodgers.

The Thursday tables, then — sixteen contests entered, and the racing lines redrawn by inches. In the American: Tampa Bay is crowned at six-and-ninety wins with the first seed; New York hosts the Wild Card round from Tuesday the nine-and-twentieth, Judge's calf willing; the Central is Cleveland's by one over Chicago with the season-series tiebreaker in the Pale Hose's keeping, and the White Sox clinch a berth with one victory or one Texas defeat; the West remains a dead heat at eight-and-seventy wins, Houston holding the Silver Boot tiebreaker with its final four at the Athletics while Texas closes against the Mets today and three at Minnesota; Toronto is eliminated, and Baltimore's thread is three games and a half with three to play. In the National: the three crowns are sewn — Atlanta, Milwaukee at nine-and-ninety wins with the bye and the hundredth win one victory away, and Los Angeles — while the wild-card row reads San Diego a game clear at the head, the Cubs and Phillies knotted at seven-and-eighty with Chicago holding both tiebreakers, and Arizona three back of the last chair; the Friars clinch with a win tonight or an Arizona defeat this afternoon. Today's bill of twelve, verified against the schedule: St. Louis at Pittsburgh at 12:35, Skenes taking the ball; the White Sox at Kansas City at 2:10 with the clinch in the air; Miami at Wrigley at 2:20, the Cubs' last home hand; the Mets at Texas at 2:35, must-win for Arlington; Arizona at Denver at 3:10, Rodriguez and his fifteen wins against the Rockies; Milwaukee at Philadelphia at 6:05 for the hundredth-win try; Cleveland at Boston at 6:45; Tampa Bay at New York at 7:05, Schlittler and his league-best 1.94 taking the ball; Cincinnati at Atlanta at 7:15; and at night's end Houston at the Athletics and the Angels at Seattle at 9:40, with San Diego at Los Angeles at 10:10. The season's last page falls Sunday the seven-and-twentieth; the Wild Card rounds open Tuesday the nine-and-twentieth. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.
