entry.title: THE CHAMPAGNE RIDES TO THE BRONX AND WAITS OUT AN AFTERNOON OF DEFIANCE — RASMUSSEN CARRIES A NO-HIT BID INTO THE SEVENTH, AND THE EAST'S CROWN IS WORN AT NIGHTFALL: RAYS 6, YANKEES 1
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 77 · Wednesday, the Three-and-Twentieth of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 15 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THE CHAMPAGNE RIDES TO THE BRONX AND WAITS OUT AN AFTERNOON OF DEFIANCE — RASMUSSEN CARRIES A NO-HIT BID INTO THE SEVENTH, AND THE EAST'S CROWN IS WORN AT NIGHTFALL: RAYS 6, YANKEES 1

Beaten in the day's opener, the Tampa men send their ace out for the nightcap and he strikes out eleven on a career-high hundred-and-fourteen pitches, no New York hit falling until the seventh; Díaz drives home four with a pair of two-run knocks; and the club picked last in March seals its fifth division title, its first since 2021, with the American's first seed besides — the one victory this paper reckoned would suffice, delivered in the second game it could reach

The plastic sheeting went up in the visitors' clubhouse at Yankee Stadium on Tuesday, and for one afternoon it hung there unemployed. Carlos Rodón, whose eight scoreless innings the card below salutes, stalled the coronation in the opener of the twin bill and sent the corks back into their crates. Whereupon the Rays handed the evening to Drew Rasmussen, and the right-hander made certain the sheeting would not hang a second day: no New York batsman touched him for a hit until the seventh inning, eleven struck out in all, and the hundred-and-fourteen pitches he spent were the most of his big-league life. The manager Boone's men managed a single run — Lombard Jr.'s knock in the seventh — and three hits the whole night.

The scoring had the patience of men who knew what waited. Vilade's groundout cashed the first run in the third; in the seventh Walls dropped a bunt single to fetch home Simpson, and Yandy Díaz lined a two-run knock that survived a New York challenge; in the ninth Díaz did it again, two more across, four driven in on the evening. Fried, who took the defeat, offered no alibi: "You don't want anyone to be celebrating at your stadium. Especially with the way Carlos came out, we wanted to put some pressure and be able to win some games. Unfortunately, I wasn't able to follow up on what he was able to do."

So the arithmetic this paper has carried all week — one Rays victory in the Bronx wears the crown — was settled by the second game it could reach. It is Tampa Bay's fifth division title in the franchise book and its first since 2021, and it carries the American's first seed, so that the league's road to the World Series now runs through the rebuilt dome where the club banked a record five-and-fifty home victories. Remember that the prognosticators of March picked these men last in a division they said belonged to any of four others. "No one really expected us to be here, so we've had to fight for it from the beginning of the season," said the veteran Martinez, who lost the afternoon game and celebrated anyway; "four teams got all the attention in this division," added the operations chief Neander, "and they're four really good teams, right? Just a testament to these guys." Even the beaten manager paid the toll honestly. "Rasmussen was great, and they've put together a fantastic regular season to earn that," said Boone. "That's theirs that they earned. Hopefully we get another crack at them in the next couple of weeks." He may have his wish; October is near enough to smell the champagne through the plastic.

News Around the League

THE OCTOBER DESK: MILWAUKEE'S BYE IS SEALED BY ATLANTA'S DEFEAT, THE NATIONAL'S WILD-CARD ROW KNOTS ITSELF AT THREE-AND-EIGHTY-SEVEN — AND THE AMERICAN'S WEST IS A DEAD HEAT WITH FIVE TO PLAY

The bye this paper has watched Milwaukee chase all week arrived Tuesday by courier: the Brewers lost at Philadelphia, but Cincinnati's whitewash of Atlanta settled the matter regardless, and Milwaukee can now finish no lower than the National's second seed. Mark the calendar as the club has — the first game of their Division Series falls on the third of October at their own American Family Field, opponent to be named by the scrambles below them. And a scramble it remains: the Cubs, beaten in twelve innings at their own park, and the Padres, whitewashed at Los Angeles, fell back into the row on the very night Philadelphia climbed, so that all three sit level at seven-and-eighty wins with five to play — the three-way knot whose written verdict this paper entered Tuesday, Chicago holding the row's head by its season series against both pursuers, Philadelphia holding the second chair over San Diego, Arizona four adrift of the field. The berth arithmetic is short: Chicago clinches a place with one victory or one Arizona defeat, and Philadelphia may clinch this very evening with a victory of its own beside an Arizona loss at Denver.

In the American, the East's coronation above leaves two live races, and neither will yield early. The West is now a dead heat at eight-and-seventy wins apiece, Houston's whitewash at Seattle and Texas's three-hit evening at Arlington having met in the middle — and the Silver Boot tiebreaker, as this paper has noted before, rests in Houston's keeping, so Houston controls its own destiny: win out, and the division is theirs. "That's what we can control," said the first baseman Walker. "We got five games ahead of us. Let's go 5-0." The Central stands as it stood: Cleveland by one over Chicago, the Guardians riding six straight and one step from a clinched berth, the White Sox riding three with the season-series tiebreaker still in their keeping. And the beaten Yankees banked their own consolation Tuesday: New York hosts the Wild Card round a second consecutive year, the first game falling on the nine-and-twentieth in the Bronx — most likely against Boston — with the survivor to open at Tampa Bay's dome on the third of October.

THE MILESTONE DESK: SEVEN STRIKEOUTS BEFORE A BREWER TOUCHED THE BALL — WHEELER'S TWO-THOUSANDTH ARRIVES IN THE FIRST INNING, AND SUÁREZ'S THREE-HUNDRED-FIFTIETH IS THROWN BACK BY A SIX-YEAR-OLD

Zack Wheeler came to the hill at Philadelphia on Tuesday needing three strikeouts to reach two thousand for his career, and had them before the first inning was out — then kept going. The first seven Milwaukee batsmen all went down on strikes, a figure no Phillies pitcher had ever matched, the punchout of Turang to close the first standing as the milestone itself. He is the six-and-ninetieth pitcher in the game's history to reach the mark, and — here is the flourish — his teammate Nola reached it earlier this same season, making the pair only the second set of teammates ever to do so in the same year, after Hudson and Peavy of the 2014 Giants. For a man whose career was twice interrupted — the elbow surgery of 2015, the blood clot and the thoracic-outlet surgery of last autumn — the figure landed sweetly. "Some of the guys asked me, 'Would you have ever thought?' And the answer is no," Wheeler said. "Just being where I am now, it's pretty special."

At Atlanta the milestone wore a party hat. Eugenio Suárez lifted his five-and-twentieth home run of the year over the left-field wall in the eighth — the three-hundred-fiftieth of his career — and the ball came down amid a birthday celebration, into the hands of a girl turning six years old that very day. Whereupon, to the astonishment of every adult in the section, she threw it back. The souvenir was lost; the memory, this paper submits, will outlast any baseball, and the Herald wishes the young fan a happy sixth.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: ACUÑA'S SHIN TAKES A FOUL AND GIVES BACK GOOD NEWS — PEDERSON'S SEASON ENDS AT THE HAND SPECIALIST'S, AND HOUSTON'S VICTORY COMES AWAY LIMPING

The gasp of the night came at Truist Park, where Ronald Acuña Jr. fouled a three-and-one cutter squarely off his own left shin in the third inning and went to the ground twice before limping off under his own power. The pictures came back kind: X-rays negative, the later scan confirming a contusion and nothing worse. "He's going to be sore. Obviously we'll err on the side of caution at this time of the year," said the manager Weiss. "But all things considered, it's good news." With the East sewn on and the third seed all but fixed, Atlanta's only remaining pennant is health; whether Acuña returns before the homestand closes Thursday will follow the swelling.

At Arlington the news ran harder. Joc Pederson, shelved since a pitch broke his left hand on the twelfth of September, progressed only as far as swings off a tee before the club conceded the regular season Tuesday and placed him on the injured list, the move dated back to the nineteenth — so that, should Texas reach the Wild Card round, he could yet be activated for it. "It just didn't progress like we hoped," said the manager Schumaker. The club also moved the pitcher Quantrill to the sixty-day shelf. And Houston's whitewash at Seattle, entered on the card below, collected its own tolls: the starter Javier departed after two innings with tightness of the right groin, and Peña and Matthews likewise left the field early, the club's five-game sprint now to be run on a trainer's-room budget.

THE CONVALESCENT DESK: THE VIGIL CLOSES TONIGHT — OHTANI IS EXPECTED IN THE LINEUP AGAINST SAN DIEGO, THOUGH PERHAPS NOT AT THE HEAD OF IT

The watch this paper has kept over Shohei Ohtani — the named series, the forty swings against the pitching-machine, the manager's Wednesday promise — reaches its final entry. "Unless I hear otherwise," said the manager Roberts on Tuesday, "he'll be in the lineup" for this evening's middle game of the San Diego series at Chavez Ravine, his fifteen-day shelf-leave expired, his return strictly as a batsman with the mound closed for the year. He is expected to play out all five remaining games to sharpen the eye he could not use from the shelf.

The one open question is the batting order's first line. With the southpaw Ray starting for San Diego, Roberts allowed he may hold Ohtani from his customary leadoff post and open instead with Betts — carrying a .984 on-base-plus-slugging figure over his last forty games — against left-handers, Ohtani taking the top spot against the right-handed kind. "That's probably the way it's going to fall out," the manager said, "but I haven't totally decided yet." The champions have scarcely suffered for the absence — three defeats in the eighteen games since he sat, and a fifth straight victory banked Tuesday by eight arms passing a shutout hand to hand, as the card relates — but October wants the whole arsenal, and tonight the largest piece steps back into the rack.

THE FAREWELL DESK: FIVE HUNDRED SEVEN-AND-FIFTY STARTS, AND THE LAST ONE NAMED — VERLANDER WILL TAKE A BIG-LEAGUE MOUND ONE FINAL TIME SATURDAY, AT THE PARK WHERE IT BEGAN

Justin Verlander walked out to the bullpen beyond the left-field fence at Comerica Park on Tuesday and threw a between-starts session, as he has done for one-and-twenty years; this one, he confirmed afterward, was the last. The club has named Saturday afternoon, against the visiting Pirates — whose series in Detroit opens Friday — for the five-hundred-fifty-seventh and final start of his career, his first outing in Tigers flannels at Comerica since August of 2017. Sidelined since March by the hip and lately the hamstring, he owned that the year broke his heart before it schooled him: "I honestly didn't envision this being the last season... [I] slowly came to the realization through the course of the year when I just couldn't get back out there." He pushed through the rehabilitation anyway, he said, for the fans as much as himself — and then, in the old competitor's registry: "Just don't do anything stupid between now and Saturday, and we should be good."

Nor will it be a ceremonial inning and a cap-wave, if the man himself has any say. "He's made it perfectly clear to me that he doesn't want the one-inning sendoff," said the manager Hinch. "He's going to give his best shot to have as close to a normal game as he can." The Herald, which has set down no small number of his deeds, will keep Saturday's account with particular care.

THE WIDER GAME: THE FIRST PENNANT OF THE WOMEN'S PROFESSIONAL LEAGUE FLIES IN LOS ANGELES — SATO THROWS THE LEAGUE'S FIRST COMPLETE GAME WITH THE TITLE ON THE LINE

History of the freshest kind was made Tuesday night in the Women's Professional Baseball League, whose inaugural season closed with a winner-take-all championship game: the Los Angeles Queens 2, the San Francisco Firebells 0, and every out of it belonging to Ayami Sato. The most decorated pitcher in the women's game — three World Cup Most Valuable awards, a pioneer season among the men of Canada's Intercounty league — had labored through the league's first summer with an earned-run figure above six and her frustrations posted plainly for all to read. With everything staked, she faced the league's heaviest-hitting club and threw the first complete game in the circuit's history, taking the championship's Most Valuable honors besides. "My mind and my pitching connected successfully, and we won," she told the crowd. "I wanted to enjoy my baseball with the best teammates in the world."

The Queens are managed, the record should note, by Eric Young Sr., late of the big-league basepaths. The Herald, a paper of the National Pastime in all its houses, tips its cap to the new champions and enters the WPBL's first pennant in the almanac with pleasure.

The Rest of the Card

RODÓN CLAIMS THE AFTERNOON FOR NEW YORK AND THE CHAMPAGNE MUST WAIT FOR DARK — EIGHT INNINGS, THREE HITS, NOT A WALK: YANKEES 2, RAYS 0

In the twin bill's opener, Carlos Rodón was everything the occasion demanded of the home nine: eight scoreless innings, three hits, eight strikeouts and not a base on balls, before Bednar sealed his five-and-thirtieth save. Bellinger's two-run blow in the fourth, his seventeenth, was the whole of the scoring off Martinez, and 41,421 saw the coronation postponed in a brisk two hours and two minutes. "It kind of sucks," the second baseman Chisholm said of the evening that followed anyway; "the end goal is the World Series, so it doesn't really affect us here."

THE AMERICAN'S TWO BEST FRESHMEN DUEL AT FENWAY AND CLEVELAND TAKES IT BY ONE — GASPER'S LATE THUNDER ANSWERED BY A NINTH-INNING SACRIFICE: FOREST CITY NINE 3, HUB NINE 2

Parker Messick against Tolle was a meeting of the league's two finest rookie arms, and the Cleveland man's five innings of one run — his fourteenth straight start of three earned or fewer, the earned-run figure now 2.55 — left with the lead. Gasper's tenth home run squared it against Gaddis in the eighth, whereupon Lowe's sacrifice fly cashed DeLauter in the ninth and Smith closed his fortieth save. A sixth consecutive victory keeps the Central's lead at one over Chicago and brings the clinch of a berth within a single step; Boston, thrice beaten running, still holds the wild-card row's second seat.

WHEELER'S RECORD FIRST INNING, MARSH'S THUNDER AT BOTH ENDS, AND A THREE-RUN EIGHTH — PHILADELPHIA MAY CLINCH TONIGHT: BROTHERLY LOVE NINE 6, MILWAUKEES 4

The milestone desk sings Wheeler's seven straight strikeouts to open; the game itself turned late. Marsh's two-run homer and Bohm's double had built a three-run lead, Milwaukee clawed level at three by the sixth — Contreras driving home all three — and then Stott lined a two-run single and Marsh a run-scoring double in the eighth, Duran sealing his three-and-thirtieth save against Lara's ninth-inning answer. The Brewers lost the game and won the bye, as the October desk relates; Philadelphia may seat itself in the wild-card row tonight with a victory beside an Arizona defeat.

ONE HIT IS ST. LOUIS'S WHOLE EVENING — JONES AND TWO RELIEF HANDS PASS THE WHITEWASH, AND PITTSBURGH MAKES IT FIVE STRAIGHT: CORSAIRS 2, CARDS 0

The Cardinals collected exactly one hit at Pittsburgh, and the Corsairs needed little more than manners to beat them: O'Hearn's single cashed Cruz in the sixth, and in the seventh the rookie Griffin stole his three-and-twentieth base and Horwitz scampered home on the wild pitch that followed. Jones took the decision, Soto sealed his sixteenth save, and Pallante — twelve victories notwithstanding — absorbed the defeat. Five straight for the Smoky City men, at eighty wins with five to play; September continues to ask their permission for nothing.

ABRAMS TWICE, AND TWICE IS PLENTY — THE SENATORS TAKE A SECOND STRAIGHT AT THE PARK LATELY RENAMED FOR A BANK: SENATORS 3, TIGERS 1

CJ Abrams supplied the entire Washington offense that mattered — a solo home run in the second, his two-and-thirtieth, and a two-run blow in the seventh, his three-and-thirtieth, with Crews aboard. Kent took the decision, Tolman his fourth save, and Detroit's answer was a single sixth-inning run. The Senators of the present day have won seven of ten while playing out the string; the Tigers, whose home is renamed for a bank from next season as this paper recorded Tuesday, drop level with them at four-and-seventy wins and turn their eyes to Saturday's farewell, entered at the desk above.

A WHITEWASH AT TRUIST AND A KEEPSAKE RETURNED TO SENDER — DE LA CRUZ AND SUÁREZ SUPPLY THE THUNDER: CINCINNATIS 4, BRAVES 0

Brandon Williamson and three relief hands blanked the crowned champions of the East on seven hits, while De La Cruz's nine-and-twentieth homer, Myers' eighth, a run-scoring single, and Suárez's milestone blow — thrown back by the birthday girl the milestone desk celebrates — built the four. Ritchie took the loss. Atlanta's evening was chiefly spent holding its breath over Acuña's shin, as the ward above relates; the Cincinnatis, playing the spoiler's part with vigor, have now blanked the Braves on the very night Milwaukee needed it done.

FIVE-AND-TWENTY RUNS, SIX THUNDERCLAPS, AND A NINTH-INNING FRIGHT — MEIDROTH DRIVES HOME FIVE AND THE SOUTH SIDERS OUTLAST THE GRAND SLAM: SOUTH SIDERS 14, ROYALS 11

The South Siders piled fourteen runs on thirteen hits at Kansas City — Meidroth's three-run homer and two-run single worth five driven in, Grichuk four hits and a trapped dive from the cycle, Murakami's three-and-thirtieth and Doyle's fourth joining the barrage, the club's ninth night this year of four home runs or more — and then held their hats through a four-run Kansas City ninth crowned by Pasquantino's grand slam. "It's the 2026 White Sox," said Vargas, the reigning Player of the Week. "We don't give up." The one-and-eightieth victory guarantees the first non-losing season on the South Side since 2022; the last wild-card chair stays warm, and Cleveland stays one game distant.

TEN INNINGS OF STALEMATE AND A SIX-RUN TWELFTH — MIAMI LEAVES WRIGLEY'S CHAMPAGNE ON ICE A SECOND NIGHT: GULF STREAM NINE 8, CUBS 2, IN TWELVE INNINGS

Stowers' twentieth homer and Ramírez's single had Miami ahead until Chicago squared it at two in the sixth; there the ledger froze for six innings, the Cubs stranding fifteen runners and going one for eighteen with men in scoring position, until the twelfth burst its seams — Conine's go-ahead knock, its run awarded when the moving pictures overturned the call at the plate, five more runs piling behind it, Mack driving home two. "We just didn't get a hit," said the manager Counsell, arithmetic enough. Four hours and ten minutes of baseball leave the North Side clinch — one win, or one Arizona defeat — waiting another day, and the wild-card row knotted as the October desk relates.

THREE HITS ARE ALL ARLINGTON CAN MUSTER AND THE WEST'S THRONE IS SHARED BY NIGHTFALL — ALVAREZ'S TWO-RUN DOUBLE TURNS THE SIXTH: METROPOLITANS 6, LONE STAR NINE 3

Texas nosed ahead on Jung's double and a pair of sacrifice flies, whereupon the Metropolitans took the evening back with three in the sixth — the catcher Alvarez lining a two-run double and scoring on Torrens' sacrifice — and Benge doubled home another in the seventh. Manaea took the decision, the loss was charged to Eovaldi, and Senga, working from the bullpen, sealed his eighth save against a Texas offense held to three hits entire. The defeat costs the Rangers sole possession of the West's throne, now shared with Houston on terms the October desk explains — and their bench loses Pederson besides, as the ward records.

THE CENTURY ARRIVES IN DENVER, AS THE LEDGER LONG PROMISED — A THREE-RUN FIRST AND ARENADO'S EIGHT-AND-TWENTIETH KEEP THE SNAKES BREATHING: SNAKES 7, MILE HIGH NINE 2

Arizona fell upon Freeland for three in the first — Moreno, Perdomo, and Carroll cashing runs nose to tail — and never looked back, Moniak adding his three-and-twentieth homer and Arenado, whose grand slam this paper sang on Monday, his eight-and-twentieth. Soroka banked his ninth victory. The defeat is Colorado's hundredth of the season — the century this paper saw standing a game away on Monday morning — and for the Snakes, four games adrift of the wild-card field with five to play, every sunrise is still a stay of execution: they must win on while Chicago, Philadelphia, and San Diego all falter.

THE MAN WHO CALLED THE MEETING SUPPLIES THE MINUTES — ALVAREZ'S ONE-AND-FORTIETH CROWNS A WHITEWASH AND HOUSTON SEIZES ITS SHARE OF THE THRONE: HOUSTON NINE 7, PUGET SOUND MEN 0

Yordan Alvarez, who stood up in the clubhouse after Sunday's sweep and demanded better, delivered it personally at Seattle: a run-scoring single in the first, his one-and-fortieth home run in the eighth — drawing level with Caminero atop the American's ledger — and three driven in toward a hundred-and-two on the year. Walker's three-run blow off Gilbert did the early heavy lifting, and after Javier's two innings ended in the trainer's room, four relief hands — the rookie Ullola taking the decision — passed the shutout home. "That's our club right there," said the manager Espada. The West is a dead heat at eight-and-seventy wins, and Houston holds the tiebreaker; the arithmetic is at the October desk.

DOWN SIX-TO-TWO AFTER SIX, AHEAD FOR GOOD BY THE EIGHTH — CORTES AND GELOF STAGE THE COMEBACK OF THE NIGHT: MACKMEN 9, HALOS 7

Anaheim built its lead on Guzman's three-run homer and led six-to-two entering the seventh, whereupon the Mackmen scored three there — Cortes tripling and coming home, McNeil walking one in with the bases full — and four more in the eighth on a pair of two-run blows, Cortes' tenth homer and Gelof's twentieth. Medina took the decision and Harris, surviving a ninth-inning run, his sixteenth save. Trout crossed the plate twice in a losing cause for the Halos, whose seven-and-ninetieth defeat keeps them two games astern of the Mackmen at the West's floor.

JENKINS'S FOURTH PROVES THE DIFFERENCE AND BRADLEY BANKS A TWELFTH — MINNESOTA SQUARES THE SERIES BY THE BAY: TWINS 3, ORANGE AND BLACK 2

A night after falling to the Giants' late-season cheer, Minnesota answered with small precision: Keaschall's triple and Lee's single built two in the sixth, the young Walker Jenkins lifted his fourth home run in the seventh, and Bradley banked his twelfth victory, Hoffman sealing his sixth save around San Francisco's ninth-inning push. The Orange and Black, whose three-and-ninetieth defeat arrived despite a spirited final week, send the rubber match to this afternoon's card.

EIGHT ARMS PASS ONE WHITEWASH HAND TO HAND — FREEMAN DRIVES HOME THREE, AND THE CHAMPIONS ROLL A FIFTH STRAIGHT ON THE EVE OF THE GREAT RETURN: BOYS IN BLUE 7, MISSION NINE 0

The champions staged a bullpen procession — eight pitchers, five San Diego hits, not a run — while the bats did brisk business against King: two bases-full walks and Freeman's two-run single made four in the second, Freeman cashed another in the fourth, and Edman's eighth homer and Smith's tenth finished the account. Wrobleski's inning took the decision to twelve victories, and Sasaki, a day off the shelf, struck out two in a clean frame of his own. Five straight for Los Angeles at seven-and-ninety wins; the Mission nine, whitewashed a night after their streak died, fall back into the wild-card knot — and tonight Ohtani is expected back in the lineup against them, as the convalescent desk relates.

The Wednesday tables, then — with the American's East decided in the Bronx. In the American: Tampa Bay is crowned at six-and-ninety wins and holds the first seed, its Division Series to open at the dome on the third of October; New York hosts the Wild Card round from the nine-and-twentieth, most likely against Boston; the Central is Cleveland's by one over Chicago, the Guardians riding six straight against the White Sox' three, with the season-series tiebreaker still in Chicago's keeping; the West is a dead heat, Houston and Texas level at eight-and-seventy wins with the Silver Boot tiebreaker Houston's; and the wild-card row reads New York and Boston seated, Chicago's last chair three clear of Texas, four of Toronto, and five of Baltimore. In the National: all three divisions are sewn — Atlanta, Milwaukee with the bye now in its pocket, and Los Angeles — and the wild-card row is a three-way knot at seven-and-eighty wins, Chicago's head chair held by the season series, Philadelphia's second held over San Diego, with Arizona four adrift and five to play; the Cubs clinch a berth with one win or one Arizona defeat, and Philadelphia may clinch tonight by winning while Arizona loses. Last evening's Toronto-at-Baltimore engagement was postponed entire, so today's bill carries a separate-admission twin bill at Camden Yards — sixteen games in all, verified against the schedule: Washington at Detroit at 1:10; the Baltimore twin bill at 1:35 and 6:35, the venerable Scherzer opening for Toronto; Minnesota at San Francisco at 3:45 for the rubber match; Milwaukee at Philadelphia at 6:40, Henderson opposing Nola with a Quaker clinch possible, alongside St. Louis at Pittsburgh; Tampa Bay at New York at 7:05, Seymour against Cole, the crown already bestowed; Cleveland at Boston at 7:10, Griffin against Gray and his seventeen victories; Cincinnati at Atlanta at 7:15, Sale taking the ball; the White Sox at Kansas City and Miami at Wrigley at 7:40; the Mets at Texas at 8:05; Arizona at Denver at 8:40; the Angels at the Athletics at 9:40; and at 10:10, Houston at Seattle beside San Diego at Los Angeles, Ray opposing Yamamoto with Ohtani expected back in harness. Four mornings remain to the season's last page on the seven-and-twentieth; the Wild Card rounds open on the nine-and-twentieth. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: THE LOUDSPEAKERS ASK IF HE REMEMBERS THE ONE-AND-TWENTIETH NIGHT OF SEPTEMBER — ALONSO ANSWERS WITH A FORTIETH HOME RUN ON THE DATE ITSELF: ORIOLES 4, BLUE JAYS 3
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 76 · Tuesday, the Two-and-Twentieth of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 3 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THE LOUDSPEAKERS ASK IF HE REMEMBERS THE ONE-AND-TWENTIETH NIGHT OF SEPTEMBER — ALONSO ANSWERS WITH A FORTIETH HOME RUN ON THE DATE ITSELF: ORIOLES 4, BLUE JAYS 3

Earth, Wind & Fire serenade every Alonso turn at the bat and the Polar Bear obliges twice, the second blow a two-run eighth-inning stroke off the submariner Rogers — only the second homer Rogers has allowed all year; Henderson stitches three hits between the thunderclaps; Yesavage, seven weeks mended of a carpentered knee, strikes out three in his return; and Toronto's October candle burns to the wick

The music department at Camden Yards spent Monday evening asking a question. Each time Pete Alonso walked to the plate, the loudspeakers gave out the old Earth, Wind & Fire number — do you remember, the twenty-first night of September? — it being, by the calendar, exactly that. Toronto had opened the proceedings rudely, three runs off Baz before the first inning was half spent — Lukes and Springer lining singles, Keys lifting a sacrifice fly — but Alonso began his reply at once, driving a solo blow to the opposite field in the home half, his nine-and-thirtieth of the year.

That Trey Yesavage threw the pitch at all was its own small dispatch: activated from the shelf that very morning, the right-hander was making his first appearance since the fourth of August, a surgeon having in the interval tidied the torn meniscus of his left knee, and he gave two innings on forty pitches with three strikeouts, Alonso's blow the only hit against him. Baz meanwhile settled into a long, patient turn — six and two-thirds innings, nothing beyond the first-frame three — while Henderson pulled the ledger closer with three hits, a triple among them and his four-and-twentieth home run in the sixth. So it stood 3-2 into the eighth, when a walk to the pinch man Franklin brought up Alonso against the submarining Tyler Rogers, a pitcher who surrendered one home run in all of last season and had allowed but one this year. Alonso turned upon the offering and sent it to left, the measuring machines calling it four hundred feet: the fortieth, two runs, the lead, the game. Cano took the decision, Garcia sealed his tenth save, and a crowd of 12,067 that had waited out a three-quarter-hour delay went home paid in full.

The figure deserves its frame. No man in the history of the Major Leagues had ever hit forty home runs in his first season in each league until Monday: Alonso struck three-and-fifty as a National League freshman in Flushing in 2019, and now forty in his first American League campaign, his hundred-and-eight runs driven in leading the league by nine besides. "He's just one of the most consistent players I've ever seen," testified Baz, the man he beat, and the manager Albernaz pronounced forty home runs in this league "really impressive," which is managerial for awe. For Toronto the arithmetic reads like a will: seven-and-seventy wins against eighty defeats, three games and a half from Chicago's last wild-card chair with five to play and no tiebreaker in hand — the formal elimination may arrive as soon as this evening — and the misfortunes compounded, Bateman leaving the game hurt after a sliding catch while the graver bulletins are entered at the ward below. "Tyler is our guy," said the manager Schneider of his submariner. "You trust him to make pitches like he has all year." The trust was honestly earned; September simply keeps its own accounts.

News Around the League

THE OCTOBER DESK: SIX ARE SEATED AND SIX CHAIRS REMAIN — THE EAST'S CROWN RIDES INTO THE BRONX ON A TWIN BILL, MILWAUKEE'S BYE HANGS ON A SINGLE RESULT, AND THE NATIONAL'S THREE-WAY KNOT NOW HAS A WRITTEN VERDICT

The final week opens in earnest tonight. Six clubs hold October tickets — Tampa Bay, New York, and Boston in the American; Atlanta, Milwaukee, and Los Angeles in the National — six more will be seated by Sunday, and only three divisions are decided entering the day. The heaviest freight rides into the Bronx, where the Rays, six clear with seven to play, carry a magic number of one into a separate-admission doubleheader: a single victory in the four-game set wears the East's crown and the league's first seed, precisely as this paper reckoned Monday. Martinez opposes Rodón in the 1:05 opener and Rasmussen — unbeaten in his starts since early July — opposes Fried in the 7:05 nightcap; New York's only remaining road to the division is a sweep of all four. "A tall order," the manager Boone allowed, though his men are resolved that no champagne be uncorked on their lawn. The visitors, for the occasion, unpack new road grays this evening — a fresh cut of an old look, the first the club has worn in years.

In the National, Milwaukee's number for the first-round bye is likewise one: any Brewer victory at Philadelphia tonight, or any Atlanta defeat by Cincinnati's visiting hand, settles it, and two more wins would give the Central its first hundred-win season since the 2016 Cubs. Beneath the crowned, the wild-card row holds its Monday shape — Cubs and Padres level at seven-and-eighty wins, Philadelphia one astern — but the league office has now published the knot's answer: should all three finish level, Chicago, holder of both season series at five games of six against San Diego and six of seven against Philadelphia, would seat itself fourth and host the Phillies in the Wild Card round, while San Diego, seeded sixth, would travel to Atlanta. The Friars' own berth number stands at two, their five-game winning streak the hottest iron in the league.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: THE CHEEKBONE'S VERDICT IS FRACTURES, BUT NO SURGEON'S KNIFE — BREGMAN MAY YET MAKE OCTOBER; CEASE'S PICTURES SHOW INFLAMMATION AND LIKELY CLOSE HIS YEAR; GUERRERO SITS A DAY

The foul ball that found Alex Bregman in the on-deck circle Sunday — entered in yesterday's ward with the verdict pending — has its verdict now, though by an odd courier: a report from ESPN's Jeff Passan, relayed Monday and not yet confirmed by the Cubs themselves, holds that the third baseman sustained multiple fractures of the face, that no surgery will be required, and that a return for the postseason remains possible. The manager Counsell's own accounting was plainer: "He had a cut under his eye. He was bleeding from his nose a little bit. It's pretty swollen." The patient, writing from his convalescence by way of the electric bulletin boards, kept it to two sentences: "Thanks for all the messages yall. I'll be back."

At Toronto, the pictures this paper awaited on Dylan Cease came back mercifully clean and cruelly timed at once: inflammation of the right shoulder, nothing structural, no knife — but the ace misses his turn this week and may not throw again in 2026, a heavy line for the first year of his seven-year, $210-million engagement, though the club expects no carryover to 2027. Should the season indeed be closed, it closes at a 2.40 earned-run figure with 239 strikeouts, a count only three Toronto seasons have ever bettered. "It's definitely a bit heavy and achy, just not normal," the man himself allowed. Vladimir Guerrero Jr., meanwhile, sat out Monday's defeat at Baltimore with the lower back that pinched him Sunday — "he's really just day to day," said the manager Schneider — and Detroit, even in a nine-run evening, lengthened its own sick list, shelving the infielder Colt Keith for ten days and the pitcher Troy Melton for fifteen.

THE CONVALESCENT DESK: THE CHAMPIONS RESTOCK THE ARSENAL — SASAKI AND PAGES STEP OFF THE SHELF, THE MORROW STILL BELONGS TO OHTANI, AND SHEEHAN LEARNS WHAT THE LEDGER PAYS FOR NINE STRIKEOUTS

Monday's transaction wire read like a quartermaster's manifest at Chavez Ravine. The champions activated Roki Sasaki from the fifteen-day list and the outfielder Andy Pages from the ten-day, and to make the room they optioned the catcher Alfonzo and Emmet Sheehan to Oklahoma City — the same Sheehan whose nine strikeouts in long relief this paper sang only yesterday. Two days from a hero's line to a bus ticket; the roster ledger pays no sentiment.

And the vigil's last station holds its schedule. The manager Roberts' stated plan, as recorded in Monday's dispatch, still names Wednesday — the middle game of San Diego's visit, which opens tonight at ten past the hour — for the activation of Shohei Ohtani, strictly as a batsman, his fifteen-day shelf-leave expiring with the date. The Padres arrive carrying five straight victories and their berth arithmetic; the champions carry four straight of their own and the deepest bench October money can mend. The collision seats itself tonight, and this paper will keep the account.

THE LAURELS DESK: THE WEEK'S GARLANDS GO TO TWO MEN THE PENNANT RACES LEAN UPON — VARGAS AND CRONENWORTH ARE NAMED PLAYERS OF THE WEEK

The league hung its weekly laurels Monday on a pair of pennant-race shoulders. Miguel Vargas of the White Sox — whose unprecedented season line this paper entered on Sunday — batted .348 for the week with three home runs, nine driven in, and two stolen bases, and takes the second Player of the Week honor of his life; his three-and-thirty homers beside twenty steals make him merely the third White Sox player ever to pair thirty with twenty, joining Magglio Ordóñez and Luis Robert Jr. in the South Side book.

And Jake Cronenworth of the Padres, who entered the week dragging a .581 on-base-plus-slugging figure, chose the hour of his club's need to bat 13-for-28 — a .464 clip — with two homers, eight driven in, and eight runs scored, the whole of it crowned by Sunday's two-homer, five-run afternoon against Miami that this paper recorded in Monday's card. It is his second such garland and his first since June of 2021, which is a long winter between wreaths; the streaking Friars will take the omen.

THE STRAW-POLL DESK: EIGHT-AND-THIRTY WRITERS, ONE NAME ON EVERY NATIONAL BALLOT — CROW-ARMSTRONG SWEEPS MLB.COM'S FINAL POLL OF THE YEAR, AND ALVAREZ HOLDS THE AMERICAN'S

MLB.com posted the final edition of its season-long Most Valuable poll — eight-and-thirty of its writers, five names apiece — and in the National the verdict wanted no arithmetic: Pete Crow-Armstrong took every one of the thirty-eight first-place votes, ahead of Ohtani, with Misiorowski and De La Cruz tied further back. The case is the season itself: the Cub leads the game in runs at 118 and extra-base hits at 83, shares the home-run lead at five-and-forty with Schwarber, and stands two thefts from the first 40-40 season in his franchise's history, as this paper counted only yesterday. In the American, Yordan Alvarez of Houston holds the poll's head with nine-and-twenty first-place votes to Caminero's seven, Witt, Schlittler, and Rice trailing.

The Herald appends its standing reminder: the poll is the writers' parlor game, and a fine one. The award belongs to the ballot — voted by the Base Ball Writers when the season ends, announced in November — and unanimity attaches to the poll, never yet to the trophy.

The Rest of the Card

ON THE DAY THE PARK TAKES A BANK'S NAME, THE MAN WEARING 53 TAKES THE EVENING — MALGERI'S THUNDER AND LEATHER CARRY THE DETROITS: DETROITS 9, NATS 2

Hours after the club announced that its home of six-and-twenty years — Comerica Park since the century opened — will be called Fifth Third Park from next season, the outfielder Ben Malgeri, who has worn No. 53 since his June summons, supplied the christening: a diving catch on a 108-mile-an-hour liner in the first, a double, and a three-run homer in the five-run fifth that broke the thing open. Báez and Torkelson added thunderclaps of their own among twelve Detroit hits, Lee's ground-rule double had opened the scoring, and Montero threw four one-hit innings of relief for his tenth victory. Washington's whole answer was Yohandy Morales' pinch-hit two-run homer in the eighth; the loss went to Herz, activated from the sixty-day shelf that very afternoon for his first turn of the year — a hard homecoming.

GILBERT'S BLOW MOVES KRUKOW TO BORROW HIS AILING PARTNER'S FAMOUS CRY — "AND IIIIT'S OUTTA HERE!" RINGS AT ORACLE PARK: FRISCO NINE 5, MINNESOTANS 2

Drew Gilbert collected three hits and drove in three — a two-run single in the second and, on the first pitch he saw from Matthews in the fifth, his eleventh home run — and up in the booth Mike Krukow, caught mid-handoff, blurted the signature call of the man whose chair sat empty: "And iiiiit's outta here!" Asked where it came from, the retiring broadcaster answered, "That's the only thing I could think of! I just stole it from my partner" — Duane Kuiper having stepped away for the cancer treatment this paper recorded yesterday, with every intention of rejoining the booth before his old friend's farewell weekend. On the field, Matthews struck out nine Frisco batsmen in five innings and lost anyway; Brooks Lee's four-and-twentieth homer survived a review and Rodriguez added a late one in the Minnesotans' four-hit evening; the newcomer Davidson, his contract purchased that morning, singled and stole the first base of his big-league life; and Beck took the decision with T. Harris sealing the save.

The Tuesday tables, then — the schedule having caught its breath on a three-game Monday, the full board of sixteen returns tonight. In the American: Tampa Bay holds the East by six over New York with seven to play apiece, and the crown may be worn by nightfall, the arithmetic standing at a single Rays victory in the Bronx; the Central is Cleveland's by one over Chicago, the Guardians riding five straight with the tiebreaker still in Chicago's keeping; the West is Texas's by one over Houston, the Rangers at an even .500 and the Silver Boot tiebreaker still Houston's; and the wild-card row reads New York and Boston seated, Chicago's last chair three clear of Houston, three and a half of Toronto, and four and a half of Baltimore. In the National: Atlanta's East is sewn on; Milwaukee, at eight-and-ninety victories, carries a bye number of one into Philadelphia; and the wild-card row reads Cubs and Padres level at seven-and-eighty — Chicago's head chair held by the season series — with Philadelphia one back in the third and Arizona four adrift, six to play. Tonight's bill, verified against the schedule: the Bronx twin bill at 1:05 and 7:05, Martinez and Rasmussen carrying the Rays against Rodón and Fried; Toronto at Baltimore at 6:35, the venerable Scherzer taking the ball with elimination in the air; Milwaukee at Philadelphia at 6:40, May opposing Wheeler with the bye in the balance, alongside St. Louis at Pittsburgh and Washington at Detroit; Cleveland at Boston at 6:45, Messick against Tolle; Cincinnati at Atlanta at 7:15; Miami at Wrigley and the White Sox at Kansas City at 7:40; the Mets at Texas at 8:05; Arizona at Denver at 8:40; Houston at Seattle and the Angels against the Athletics at 9:40; Minnesota at San Francisco at 9:45; and San Diego at Los Angeles at 10:10, King taking the ball for the streaking Friars. Five mornings remain to the season's last page on the seven-and-twentieth; the Wild Card rounds open on the nine-and-twentieth. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: THE CAST-OFF OF APRIL STARTS THE CLINCHER OF SEPTEMBER — A SEVENTH EAST FLAG IN NINE YEARS IS SEWN ON AT HOUSTON: BRAVES 4, ASTROS 2
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 75 · Monday, the One-and-Twentieth of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 15 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THE CAST-OFF OF APRIL STARTS THE CLINCHER OF SEPTEMBER — A SEVENTH EAST FLAG IN NINE YEARS IS SEWN ON AT HOUSTON: BRAVES 4, ASTROS 2

Pérez, judged surplus in the spring, keeps the ledger close; Yastrzemski's three-run thunder in the sixth — his third blow of the road trip — overturns Altuve's early lead; Mederos takes the decision, Dodd the save, and the sweep is complete; Houston, beaten a third straight time, sits a game off the West's throne with the wild-card ground shrinking beneath it

On the twelfth of April the Atlanta club looked upon Martín Pérez — a non-roster man of the spring — and designated him for assignment, which is the game's politest way of saying not wanted. On Sunday afternoon at Houston the same Pérez took the ball in the game that decided the National League's East, and kept it close enough for the deciding to be done. The manager Weiss has reminded his men all summer that the prognosticators wanted no part of them in March; it was fitting, then, that the flag was clinched behind a pitcher the ledger itself had once declined.

The afternoon's accounting was patient. Altuve's sixteenth home run had Houston ahead in the fourth, and ahead the Texans remained until the sixth, when Atlanta put four across in a single frame — the heart of them a three-run blast from Mike Yastrzemski, his twelfth of the year and his third of a road trip that went 4-and-2, with Albies driving home the fourth. A man bearing that name has hit October thunder before; the family trade continues. Mederos, in relief, took the decision at 5-and-1, Smith-Shawver and Kerr passed the late innings hand to hand, and Dodd sealed his second save, Diaz's eighth-inning blow the whole of Houston's answer. Four runs on six hits, not an error in the field — economy itself.

So the clinch this paper forecast Sunday morning arrived by Sunday evening, and by Atlanta's own hand: a 4-2 victory, a sweep of the Astros in their own park, and a seventh division title in the past nine years. "We've been fighting all year to get to this moment," said Pérez, and appended the sentence Atlanta will carry into October: "And we're not done yet." As the seedings stand this morning the Braves are the National's third seed, their Wild Card opponent to be drawn from among the Padres, Cubs, and Phillies — the arithmetic of that row is sorted at the October desk below. Houston's troubles, meanwhile, compound: a third straight defeat drops the Texans a game behind Texas in the West — the throne that has changed hands thrice in three mornings stays with Arlington a second day, both claimants having lost — and their grip on the wild-card row is now three games short of Chicago's chair with six to play.

News Around the League

THE OCTOBER DESK: BOSTON CLINCHES BY LOSING, TAMPA BAY MAKES A FORTRESS OF ITS DOME — AND THE CROWN MAY PASS THROUGH THE BRONX AS SOON AS TOMORROW

The strangest celebration of the year unfolded in the visitors' clubhouse at St. Petersburg, where the Red Sox — beaten 5-1 by the Rays an hour earlier — learned that Houston's defeat at Atlanta had punched their postseason ticket regardless, and set the Bee Gees' "Stayin' Alive" playing on what witnesses describe as an endless loop. A club that spent its first three months among the American's also-rans is October-bound; the berth is the reward of the long climb back, and no man in the room apologized for the scoreboard's assistance.

Their hosts, meanwhile, closed the home ledger in state. Tampa Bay's 5-1 decision was its five-and-fiftieth victory of the year in the rebuilt dome — a single-season record for the house — capping an 8-and-1 homestand that included three walk-off victories. The East's lead stands at six with seven to play, and the arithmetic now runs through the Bronx: the Rays need but one victory in the four-game set at Yankee Stadium that opens with Tuesday's doubleheader to wear the division's crown and the league's first seed. In the National, the row beneath the champions re-sorts nightly: the Cubs and Padres sit level at seven-and-eighty wins, Chicago holding the row's head by its season series against both San Diego and Philadelphia; the Padres — winners of thirteen of fourteen, the hottest club in the land — carry a magic number of two toward a third consecutive postseason, a thing never once managed in the franchise's eight-and-fifty seasons; and Milwaukee, its franchise record already banked as the card below relates, needs but one more victory — or one more Atlanta defeat — to claim the National's first-round bye. Both clubs stand idle this day, so that question keeps until Tuesday.

THE MILESTONE DESK: TWENTY-AND-TWENTY, TWICE OVER — CHOURIO WRITES A LINE NO MAN HIS AGE EVER WROTE, AND CRUZ JOINS BONDS AND McCUTCHEN IN THE PITTSBURGH BOOK

History was made at Camden Yards by way of a walk and a dash. When Jackson Chourio stole second in the sixth inning Sunday — safe upon appeal to the moving pictures, the first call having gone against him — the theft was his twentieth of the season, set beside four-and-twenty home runs, and made him the first player in Major League history to complete three 20-20 campaigns before his twenty-third birthday. Only Julio Rodríguez of Seattle and Bobby Witt Jr. of Kansas City have so much as opened their careers with three straight such seasons, and neither did it so young. "That's just Chourio," shrugged his old bush-league mate Misiorowski. "He's an animal out there." The Wonder Kid stole another base later in the evening for good measure.

And at Pittsburgh, Oneil Cruz heard the two names he had just joined and paused a full ten seconds before speaking. His fourth-inning blast off Wacha — a 75-mile-an-hour curveball dispatched 420 feet to dead center — was his twentieth home run, making him merely the third Pirate ever to pair twenty homers with twenty steals in three consecutive seasons. The others are Barry Bonds and Andrew McCutchen. That Cruz has done it in three-and-ninety games, two months of his summer lost to a fractured hand, only sharpens the figure; since his August return he bats .318 and slugs .533, and his club — 52-and-41 with him, 27-and-36 without — has won four straight, as the card relates.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: A FOUL BALL FINDS THE MAN WAITING HIS TURN — BREGMAN CARTED TO THE HOSPITAL FROM THE ON-DECK CIRCLE, AND TORONTO'S SICK LIST LENGTHENS BY TWO

The ugliest moment of the Sunday card involved no pitch thrown in anger. In the fourth inning at Cincinnati, Alex Bregman stood in the on-deck circle when his teammate Busch half-swung at an offering from Mey and fouled it squarely into Bregman's left cheekbone. The third baseman walked to the dugout under his own power, was lifted for a pinch-hitter, and was sent to the hospital for X-rays and further examination; the club had no verdict by night's end. "Any time the ball hits the head area, it's scary," said Busch, who bore the guiltless guilt of the man at the plate. "You focus on the game, but it's tough." The Cubs won the game 9-1, and would trade the margin entire for a clean bill.

Toronto's troubles wear no bandage so visible but run deeper into the pitching ledger. Dylan Cease, the staff's ace, has been sent back to Toronto for an examination of his throwing shoulder and is scratched from his Wednesday turn, the club awaiting the pictures before speaking of a return; and Vladimir Guerrero Jr. left Sunday's victory at Arlington in the fourth inning with tightness of the lower back — "we just wanted to be careful," said the manager Schneider, "and hopefully he's good for tomorrow." For a club three games shy of the wild-card row's last chair, every man on the table is a game off the ledger.

THE CONVALESCENT DESK: WEDNESDAY IS NAMED FOR THE GREAT RETURN — OHTANI'S SHELF-LEAVE EXPIRES MIDWEEK, WHILE SKUBAL STEPS AWAY ON A FAMILY MATTER AND THE CHAMPIONS SHUFFLE THEIR DECK

The vigil this paper has kept over Shohei Ohtani's recovery may close midweek. The manager Roberts, having promised Saturday that the returning series was at hand, has now named the day: there is "a good chance" the great man is activated Wednesday, when his fifteen-day shelf-leave — dated back to the eighth of September — expires, in the second game of San Diego's visit to Chavez Ravine. He returns strictly as a batsman, the mound closed for his year, and the swings taken against the pitching-machine that throws like a big-leaguer have all come away satisfactory.

The same champions spent Sunday shuffling the deck around him. Tarik Skubal went to the bereavement list on a family matter — "he's fine," Roberts assured, and the leave may cost him no turn at all, his next start projected for Friday at San Francisco — while Sheehan and Hurt came up from Oklahoma City, and Sheehan promptly struck out nine Giants across a long scoreless relief, as the card below admires. Tucker, nursing a leg bruised by his own foul ball Saturday, sat the start and then pinch-hit anyway. The champions won their fourth straight all the same; whole in October is the only wholeness they are counting.

THE BROADCAST BOOTH: KUIPER TAKES THE HARD NEWS STANDING — A SECOND BOUT WITH CANCER ANNOUNCED, AND A VOW TO CALL HIS OLD FRIEND'S FAREWELL

Sad tidings from the Bay, borne with the steadiness of a man who has sat before a microphone for decades. Duane Kuiper, six-and-seventy years old and the voice of the Giants for a generation, announced Sunday that he has been diagnosed with throat cancer — an illness unrelated, his physicians say, to the cancer he fought and beat in 2021 — and that treatment at Stanford began last week. "I'm optimistic that it will be successfully treated," he said, and the paper takes him at his word.

The timing is its own small heartbreak: the booth beside him belongs to Mike Krukow, his friend of forty years, who retires when this season ends after six-and-thirty years behind the microphone. Kuiper had hoped to call the weekend's games at Los Angeles and could not travel; he plans instead to return to the booth Tuesday, and to call the season's closing series against the Dodgers at Oracle Park — the sendoff, he means to say, will not go unvoiced. The Herald, which trades daily in the sound of the game, tips its hat to a man who has supplied so much of it, and wishes him the swift and total recovery the record says he knows how to make.

The Rest of the Card

SÁNCHEZ BANKS AN EIGHTEENTH AND SCHWARBER WALKS FOUR TIMES WITHOUT SWINGING AT ANYTHING USEFUL — THE QUAKERS TAKE THE FLUSHING FINALE: QUAKERS 7, METS 2

Cristopher Sánchez worked deep into the evening for his eighteenth victory against six defeats, while Philadelphia's patience did the scoring — nine walks drawn in all, four of them by Schwarber alone — and Crawford tripled and drove home three. Bichette's seventeenth home run supplied the whole of the Flushing answer; the Quakers hold the National's third wild-card chair, one game astern of the row's co-leaders, with the champions of Milwaukee arriving Tuesday.

CRUZ'S TWENTIETH IN THE FOURTH, FLORES JR.'S ANSWER IN THE EIGHTH — THE BUCS SWEEP KANSAS CITY AND MAKE IT FOUR STRAIGHT: BUCS 4, ROYALS 3

Pasquantino's two-run blow in the seventh had put Kansas City ahead 3-2, whereupon the rookie Rafael Flores Jr. struck a two-run homer in the eighth — his tenth — to take it back for good. Cruz's milestone thunder, enshrined at the desk above, had kept the ledger close; Mlodzinski took the decision and Montgomery sealed his sixteenth save, and Pittsburgh, at nine-and-seventy wins with six to play, is assembling a September nobody asked its permission for.

NINE STRIKEOUTS, THREE HITS, AND THE STRIKEOUT CROWN RECLAIMED — WILLIAMS SENDS THE CLEVELAND NINE HOME IN FRONT: CLEVELAND NINE 1, ATHLETICS 0

Gavin Williams gave seven innings of three hits and a lone walk, struck out nine to retake the American's strikeout lead, and left the rest to Adell — whose fourth-inning knock drove home run number three-and-ninety of his season, the game's only tally — and to Smith, whose nine-and-thirtieth save closed the sweep. "You can kind of see the panic in a lot of the hitters," observed Kwan. Five straight victories send Cleveland on the road holding the Central by one over Chicago; the Athletics, whitewashed, have dropped six straight.

FOUR IN THE FIRST AND THE DOME'S LEDGER CLOSES AT FIVE-AND-FIFTY — THE SUNSHINE NINE BID THEIR HOUSE FAREWELL IN STATE: SUNSHINE NINE 5, CRIMSON HOSE 1

Tampa Bay fell upon Sandoval for four runs before the first inning was out — DeLuca and Simpson driving home two apiece, Mesa Jr. adding his fourteenth homer later — and Jax with five relief hands behind him kept Boston to a single ninth-inning run on Story's fifth. The victory was the record fifty-fifth in the dome this season and the defeated clinched anyway, as the October desk relates — a game whose loser left in champagne, which even this correspondent's archives cannot precedent. Simpson's stolen base was his six-and-fortieth.

A TRIPLE SHY OF THE CYCLE AND TWO SHY OF FORTY-AND-FORTY — CROW-ARMSTRONG'S FIVE-AND-FORTIETH POWERS THE ROUT AT CINCINNATI: CUBS 9, REDLEGS 1

Pete Crow-Armstrong, hitless the two days prior, answered with three hits — single, double, and his five-and-fortieth home run, the triple alone withheld — stole his eight-and-thirtieth base to stand two thefts from the first 40-40 season in the franchise book, and drove in two of Chicago's nine. Suzuki's five-and-twentieth and Conforto's fifteenth joined the barrage; Peterson took his ninth win; Bregman's run-scoring single preceded the misfortune the infirmary ward records, and the Cubs' clinch-watch continues, Arizona's victory having kept the champagne corked a day.

THE RAIN DELAY OUTLASTED THE BASEBALL, AND THE BASEBALL WAS ALL CHICAGO'S — MEIDROTH'S THUNDER KEEPS THE LAST CHAIR WARM: WHITE STOCKINGS 8, BENGALS 1

The crowd waited out three hours and fifty minutes of weather to see two hours and fifty of baseball, and the White Stockings made the arithmetic worth it: Meidroth homered and drove in two, Antonacci matched him with two of his own and a stolen base besides, and Murakami and Grichuk added knocks in a ten-hit evening while Detroit managed a single late run. Brazobán took the decision in relief. Chicago thus holds the American's final wild-card chair by three over Toronto and Houston, one game off Cleveland's Central lead — every road still open.

HERRERA STRIKES TWICE AND THE BOY BERNAL BREAKS IT LATE — A THREE-RUN EIGHTH SENDS THE CAPITAL NINE HOME EMPTY: REDBIRDS 5, CAPITAL NINE 3

Iván Herrera homered twice — his seventeenth and eighteenth — yet Washington stood a run ahead entering the eighth, whereupon St. Louis put three across, Bernal's fourth home run the loudest of the blows. Gastelum took the decision and O'Brien sealed his eight-and-thirtieth save, most in the National; Abrams answered for Washington with his one-and-thirtieth homer and three-and-thirtieth steal in a losing cause.

FOUR IN THE SEVENTH UNDO deGROM AND THE SWEEP IS AVOIDED — TORONTO'S CANDLE GUTTERS BUT DOES NOT GO OUT: BLUE JAYS 7, RANGERS 2

Toronto nicked single runs through the early innings, absorbed Burger's two-run seventh-and-twentieth homer, and then broke the thing open with four in the seventh — McAdoo and Lukes driving home two apiece on the night, Clement's two-and-thirtieth double among eleven Toronto hits. Arrighetti took the decision in relief; deGrom was charged with his tenth defeat against eleven victories. The Jays, three back of the last chair, stay mathematically breathing — though Guerrero's fourth-inning exit, recorded at the infirmary ward, shadowed the win. Texas, beaten, keeps the West's throne by a game only because Houston fell the same afternoon.

SEVEN SCORELESS IN THE MOUNTAIN AIR FROM A MAN A MONTH IN THE LEAGUE — ANDERSON MAKES COORS FIELD SIT QUIETLY: SEATTLE NINE 2, ROCKIES 1

Kade Anderson, called up only in late August, gave the start of his young life where pitching goes to die: seven innings at Denver, three hits, no walks, seven strikeouts, not a run, and all of it on four-and-eighty pitches. Canzone drove home both Seattle runs; Goodman's nine-and-thirtieth homer in the ninth spoiled the whitewash before Bazardo banked his first save. The Rockies' ninety-ninth defeat leaves them a game from the century; Seattle plays out the string with its eyes openly on 2027 — "and beyond," as the wires put it.

TWO HITS ARE ALL ANAHEIM CAN SHOW FOR NINE INNINGS — KREMER AND OBER PASS THE WHITEWASH BETWEEN THEM, AND RODEN DRIVES HOME FOUR: TWIN CITIES NINE 8, SERAPHS 0

Kremer carried the shutout deep and Ober carried it home, two Anaheim hits the entire evening's yield, while Minnesota's thirteen hits included the young Roden's first home run of the campaign in a four-run night's work, Bell driving home two more and the rookie Ross logging his first steal and first run driven in of the season besides. The Twin Cities men square their account at the season's margin; the Seraphs absorb defeat six-and-ninety, whitewashed a second time in three nights.

CRONENWORTH TWICE, TATIS ONCE, AND THE DRUM ROLLS ON — THIRTEEN WINS IN FOURTEEN, AND THE MAGIC NUMBER READS TWO: PADRES 7, MARLINS 3

Jake Cronenworth homered twice and drove in five — a season's work in an evening — and Tatis added his five-and-twentieth as San Diego banked a fifth consecutive victory, Buehler taking the decision. Sanoja's three-run seventh-inning homer was the whole of Miami's reply. The Friars' arithmetic is entered at the October desk: no club in the land is hotter, and no Padres club in eight-and-fifty years has reached October three years running — a drought two victories from its end.

FOUL BY FEET, THEN FAIR BY PLENTY — ARENADO'S SECOND-CHANCE SLAM OVERTURNS THE AFTERNOON, AND THE DESERT NINE REFUSE THE UNDERTAKER A DAY LONGER: DESERT NINE 8, YANKEES 4

New York's third inning produced three home runs nose to tail — Ramos, the boy Lombard Jr., and Jones — and a 4-1 lead that lasted precisely until Nolan Arenado came up with the bases full in the fifth. His first blast hooked foul at the pole; the next pitch he hammered fair into the left-field seats — a grand slam, his ninth of a career and third of the season, tying the franchise's single-season record — crowning a five-run frame in the club's forty-seventh comeback victory of the year, most in the Majors. Perdomo tripled and drove home two more. The Desert nine remain four back of the last chair with six to play — alive, which was Sunday's entire object; the Yankees, still without their captain, dropped a second straight.

NINE STRIKEOUTS FROM THE MAN RECALLED AT NOON — SHEEHAN'S LONG RELIEF CARRIES THE ANGELENOS PAST THE BAY NINE: ANGELENOS 3, BAY NINE 1

Recalled from Oklahoma City in the morning's shuffle, Emmet Sheehan was in a big-league game by afternoon and struck out nine San Francisco batsmen across a long scoreless relief, the visitors' first-inning run standing alone all day. Los Angeles chipped a run apiece from the sixth, seventh, and eighth — Edman's seventh homer among them — with Bubic taking the decision and Scott his three-and-twentieth save. A fourth straight victory for the crowned champions of the West, who now await Wednesday's reinforcement as the convalescent desk relates; the Bay nine have lost two-and-ninety.

THREE INNINGS BY DESIGN FOR THE ACE, A RECORD BY RIGHT FOR THE CLUB — VICTORY EIGHT-AND-NINETY STANDS ALONE IN THE CREAM CITY BOOK: CREAM CITY NINE 3, ORIOLES 0

Misiorowski threw three sharp innings and departed exactly on schedule — nothing wrong, the club hastened to say, but a bringing-in of the great arm for its safe October landing — and six relief hands finished the whitewash, Hall taking the decision and Megill his nine-and-twentieth save. Contreras homered, the rookie shortstop Pratt singled home two, and Chourio ran into history as the milestone desk sings. Victory eight-and-ninety breaks the franchise record Milwaukee had only just tied, with six games yet to play and the first-round bye a single result away — the October desk holds that arithmetic.

The Monday tables, then — with two flags decided and a third near. In the American: Tampa Bay, its home ledger closed at a record five-and-fifty wins in the dome, leads clinched New York by six and may take the East with a single victory in the Bronx, where a doubleheader opens the four-game set Tuesday; the Central is Cleveland's by one over Chicago; the West is Texas's by one over Houston, both having lost Sunday, the Silver Boot tiebreaker still in Houston's keeping; and the wild-card row reads New York and Boston seated — Boston's ticket punched Sunday by Houston's defeat — with Chicago's last chair three clear of Toronto and Houston alike. In the National: Atlanta's East is sewn on, as the day's chief dispatch relates; Milwaukee, its franchise record standing at eight-and-ninety victories, needs one more win or one Atlanta defeat for the bye, and two more wins for the Central's first hundred-win season since the 2016 Cubs; the champions of the West have won four straight; and the wild-card row reads Cubs and Padres level at seven-and-eighty — Chicago's head chair held by the season series — with Philadelphia one back in the third and Arizona four adrift with six to play. Today's bill is a thin Monday card of three, verified against the schedule: Toronto at Baltimore at 6:35, Yesavage opposing Baz; Washington at Detroit at 6:40; and Minnesota at San Francisco at 9:45. Tomorrow the full board returns — the Bronx twin bill from 1:05, Milwaukee at Philadelphia with the bye perhaps in the balance, Cincinnati at Atlanta, and San Diego at Los Angeles with the Friars' magic number at two. Six mornings remain to the season's last page on the seven-and-twentieth; the Wild Card rounds open on the nine-and-twentieth. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.
